findings.title: [H01] Inconsistencies in stored data may lead to incorrect median price
findings.root_cause: The DelFiPrice contract has a public prices mapping intended to store the median price for each asset. Following the specification, an asset is referenced by its symbol (a string in uppercase letters) and the corresponding median price is stored as a uint64 value.
findings.body:
### [H01] Inconsistencies in stored data may lead to incorrect median price

The DelFiPrice contract has a public prices mapping intended to store the median price for each asset. Following the specification, an asset is referenced by its symbol (a string in uppercase letters) and the corresponding median price is stored as a uint64 value. Anyone can post prices on chain, but only those signed by trusted sources are taken into account when calculating the median price. There are two ways to post an asset’s price on chain.

The first method is via the external put function of the OpenOraclePriceData contract. Given a signature and the associated message containing the price and the asset’s symbol (among other things), the function will first recover the source from the message and signature, and then update the asset’s price for this particular source. Price data for each source and symbol is kept in the contract’s storage in private data mapping. Note that prices updated via this method do not trigger a recalculation of the official (median) price hold in the public prices mapping of the DelFiPrice contract. As a consequence, if at this point a user queries an asset’s price reading the prices mapping, the returned median price will be incorrect. Furthermore, if the user queries the asset’s price using the medianPrice function, the returned median price may be inaccurate as well, since it will not be compared against the anchor price to validate it.

The other way to submit prices is via the external postPrices function of the DelFiPrice, which allows to report a batch of prices (with associated signatures) of one or more assets in a single transaction. Internally, postPrices calls the put function. In this case, the postPrices function also correctly recalculates the median price of each asset passed in the symbols parameter, updating the corresponding entries in the prices mapping if the median is within safe bounds. However, if there is a mismatch between the assets referenced in the symbols array and the assets which prices were updated, then some median prices will not be recalculated.

According to the specification, “Whenever a post happens, the official (median) price is recalculated”. This is not strictly followed by the current implementation, leaving the door open for potential data inconsistencies in the registered prices and their medians. Taking into account that reporting accurate median prices is the fundamental purpose of the system, we understand this to be a High severity issue. Consider applying the necessary modifications to strictly follow the specification. In particular, there should be a single reliable way to post prices on chain, and a single reliable way to query the median price for an asset.

## Medium severity

findings.root_cause: The “official” price reported by the Open Oracle consists of the median price calculated over a set of individual prices reported by trusted sources. As it is known, the actual prices of most cryptocurrency-related assets are highly volatile, prone to suffer sudden, extreme and unpredictable fluctuations in short periods of time.
findings.body:
### [M01] Potentially inaccurate median price during sudden, extreme, price variations

The “official” price reported by the Open Oracle consists of the median price calculated over a set of individual prices reported by trusted sources. As it is known, the actual prices of most cryptocurrency-related assets are highly volatile, prone to suffer sudden, extreme and unpredictable fluctuations in short periods of time.

Since the prices reported by the Open Oracle are based on the median of a set of individual prices, the oracle needs at least 50% of the individual prices to be accurate for the median to be accurate as well. In an event of a sudden, extreme, asset price variation, the median price reported by the oracle would only reflect the new price once 50% of the sources report on the new price. As a consequence, the Open Oracle may not reflect sudden, extreme, variations in a timely manner. This behavior becomes more problematic at times when the Ethereum network is highly congested, since transactions reporting newer prices will take longer than usual to be mined. Projects relying on the Open Oracle feed must be aware of the associated risks during times of high price volatility, and implement the necessary logic to adapt to potential delays in the prices reported by the oracle.

To better reflect price variations, consider not only calculating the median of the individual prices reported for a given asset, but also computing their standard deviation. This should favor the oracle’s transparency, and help projects querying the Open Oracle better understand the actual distribution of the prices, thus allowing them to take more informed decisions.

findings.title: [M02] Lack of minimum sample size requirement for official price calculation
findings.root_cause: To obtain the official price for an asset, Compound’s Open Oracle takes all reported price data from trusted sources, calculates a median price using the medianPrice function of the DelFiPrice contract, and finally supplies this median price as the asset’s price.
findings.body:
### [M02] Lack of minimum sample size requirement for official price calculation

To obtain the official price for an asset, Compound’s Open Oracle takes all reported price data from trusted sources, calculates a median price using the medianPrice function of the DelFiPrice contract, and finally supplies this median price as the asset’s price.

However, this process does not take into account the sample size of the prices when calculating the median price of an asset, which may render the oracle vunerable to a price manipulation attack when the sample size is low (see [N09] Considerations on rogue sources note for a more detailed description).

Consider either implementing a minimum sample size requirement or returning the sample size together with the oracle’s official price, so as to raise awareness on the potential risks when the sample size is dangerously low.

findings.title: [M03] Function put allows storing invalid signed data
findings.root_cause: The put function of the OpenOraclePriceData is used to submit signed price data. It first recovers the signing address from the given signature and message by means of the inherited source function, and then uses the recovered address (i.e., the source) to update the price and timestamp under the corresponding source address and asset symbol.
findings.body:
### [M03] Function put allows storing invalid signed data

The put function of the OpenOraclePriceData is used to submit signed price data. It first recovers the signing address from the given signature and message by means of the inherited source function, and then uses the recovered address (i.e., the source) to update the price and timestamp under the corresponding source address and asset symbol.

The inherited source function uses the ecrecover precompile to recover the signing address. If there is an error during the recovering process, ecrecover will return the zero address (as stated in its documentation). Since the returned address is never validated in the put function, this could lead to submitting invalid data with a successful transaction. While this does not pose a security risk, since data would be written in an entry corresponding to the zero address, the function should fail earlier to favor a more predictable behavior.

Consider ensuring the address returned by the source function is not the zero address before continuing execution in the put function.

findings.title: [M04] Oracle might fail if anchor price is not updated fast enough
findings.root_cause: The DelFiPrice contract implements a safety mechanism to disregard reports that, while coming from trusted sources, may lead to a drastic variation of the official median price reported by the oracle. The mechanism is based on an anchor price (reported by a trusted anchor address), together with upper and lower bounds that calculated median prices are checked against.
findings.body:
### [M04] Oracle might fail if anchor price is not updated fast enough

The DelFiPrice contract implements a safety mechanism to disregard reports that, while coming from trusted sources, may lead to a drastic variation of the official median price reported by the oracle. The mechanism is based on an anchor price (reported by a trusted anchor address), together with upper and lower bounds that calculated median prices are checked against. Should the ratio between a new median price and the anchor price be out-of-bounds, the official median price of the asset would not be updated. Both the address that reports the anchor price and the tolerance allowed between the anchor and the median are set during construction.

In an scenario of high price volatility, a trusted source may report a sharp variation of an asset’s price. As a consequence, the newly calculated median price may easily fall out of the acceptable range defined by the anchor price. Unless the anchor value is rapidly updated by the trusted anchor address, the oracle will never accept the new median price, thus causing the oracle to fail.

The address in charge of reporting the anchor price plays a fundamental role in the Open Oracle system, particularly in times of steep price variations. While the way this address is managed is out of this audit’s scope, we strongly advise closely monitoring price fluctuations and trends, so as to be able to quickly update the anchor price record and ensure the oracle prices can always be correctly updated.

## Low severity

findings.title: Attacker-controlled payer_position injects relayer's payer signer into arbitrary CPI, enabling theft of relayer funds
findings.root_cause: The on_recv_packet instruction handler in the ics27-gmp program builds a CPI instruction from the IBC packet data GmpSolanaPayload, which contains • data, instruction bytes, • accounts, account metas, and • payer_position, an index at which to inject the relayer's fee payer.
findings.body:
[C-1] Attacker-controlled payer_position injects relayer's payer
              signer into arbitrary CPI, enabling theft of relayer funds

                SEVERITY: Critical                                   IMPACT: High


                STATUS: Resolved                                     LIKELIHOOD: High




              Target
               • programs/solana/programs/ics27-gmp/src/instructions/on_recv_packet.rs#L178-L186



              Description:
              The on_recv_packet instruction handler in the ics27-gmp program builds a CPI instruction
              from the IBC packet data GmpSolanaPayload, which contains
               • data, instruction bytes,
               • accounts, account metas, and
               • payer_position, an index at which to inject the relayer's fee payer.

              The relayer's payer is inserted as AccountMeta/:new(payer, true) (writable + signer) at the
              attacker-chosen index, and signer privilege propagates through Solana's CPI mechanism.
              This allows an attacker to craft a GMP packet that executes a CPI to any program with the
              relayer's fee payer authority, enabling theft of funds (both SOL and SPL tokens) from the
              relayer.
              No restriction exists on which program the packet can target, i.e., which program the CPI
              will call.

              A straightforward exploit targets the system program and transfers the relayer's SOL to the
              attacker:

              1. Attacker sends a GMP packet with receiver = System Program ID.
              2. accounts contains a single entry: the attacker's SOL account (writable).
              3. payer_position = 0, placing the relayer as the first account.
              4. data encodes a system program Transfer instruction.

 COSMOS LABS     SMART CONTRACT SECURITY ASSESSMENT                                            VERSION 1.1




              The GMP program validates only the attacker's account (trivially matches), then inserts the
              relayer at index 0. The final CPI becomes SystemProgram/:Transfer { from: RELAYER,
              to: ATTACKER }. The relayer signed the outer transaction, so the system program accepts
              it.

              The injected payer is the relayer's single global fee payer keypair. An address configured in
              CosmosToSolanaConfig.solana_fee_payer and reused across all transactions. This means
              that the relayer's entire operational wallet balance is at risk.
              Similarly, the router program's packet callbacks (recv_packet, ack_packet, and
              timeout_packet) forward relayer-controlled signer authority into registered IBC app CPIs.
              However, such IBC apps are not arbitrary and must be registered by the permissioned
              ID_CUSTOMIZER_ROLE role.



              Recommendations:
              Consider re-architecting the rent payment. For example, replacing the relayer payer
              injection with the per-user GMP Account PDA as the rent payer. Since it already signs via
              invoke_signed, pre-funding it with SOL allows it to pay rent without exposing the relayer's
              signer to attacker-controlled CPIs.

              Cosmos Labs: Resolved with @151b171433//. and @baf0811d59//.
              Zenith: Verified.

findings.title: Ed25519 pre�verification PDAs trusted as final truth in Solana Tendermint light client
findings.root_cause: SolanaSignatureVerifier treats sig_verify PDAs as an authoritative oracle for Ed25519 validity: if a PDA at PDA(["sig_verify", sha256(pk‖msg‖sig)], program_id) has is_valid /= 1 at the expected offset, the verifier unconditionally accepts the signature and skips brine_ed25519 verification.
findings.body:
[H-1] Ed25519 pre�verification PDAs trusted as final truth in
              Solana Tendermint light client

                SEVERITY: High                                   IMPACT: Informational


                STATUS: Resolved                                 LIKELIHOOD: Low




              Target
               • packages/tendermint-light-client/solana/src/lib.rs
               • programs/ics07-tendermint/src/instructions/pre_verify_signatures.rs
               • packages/relayer/modules/cosmos-to-solana/src/tx_builder/client.rs


              Description:
              SolanaSignatureVerifier treats sig_verify PDAs as an authoritative oracle for Ed25519
              validity: if a PDA at PDA(["sig_verify", sha256(pk‖msg‖sig)], program_id) has is_valid
              /= 1 at the expected offset, the verifier unconditionally accepts the signature and skips
              brine_ed25519 verification.

              Those PDAs are created by the ICS07 program’s pre_verify_signature instruction, which:
               • Derives the same signature_hash,
               • Calls the Ed25519 precompile, but only checks bytes inside instruction 0 and ignores
                 the *_instruction_index fields that tell the precompile where it actually read
                 pubkey/msg/signature from.

              A malicious relayer can craft a transaction in which:
               • The Ed25519 precompile verifies some benign (pk₂, msg₂, sig₂) from another
                 instruction, while
               • Instruction 0 contains attacker�chosen (pk₁, msg₁, sig₁) matching SignatureData.

              pre_verify_signature will mark (pk₁, msg₁, sig₁) as is_valid = 1, and
              SolanaSignatureVerifier will later accept those forged signatures as if they were
              genuinely precompiled. This allows such a relayer to:
               • Make the Tendermint client accept arbitrary fabricated headers/commits,

 COSMOS LABS     SMART CONTRACT SECURITY ASSESSMENT                                            VERSION 1.1




               • Drive the client state (heights, timestamps, app hashes) to attacker�chosen values, and
               • Thus forge IBC membership/non�membership proofs and misbehaviour outcomes on
                 Solana.


              Recommendations:
              We recommend aligning the producer with the verifier’s assumptions:
               • Make pre_verify_signature either:
                  • Enforce *_instruction_index /= u16/:MAX and that the Ed25519 instruction is
                    instruction 0, or
                  • Explicitly validate that the same instruction and offsets used by the precompile are
                    the ones being checked for (pk,msg,sig).
               • Reject any Ed25519 instruction where these invariants are not met.

              Cosmos Labs: Resolved with @86505ac8c6//.

              Zenith: Verified.

 COSMOS LABS     SMART CONTRACT SECURITY ASSESSMENT                                            VERSION 1.1

findings.title: Relayer-controlled metadata port routes packets to the wrong IBC application, breaking core routing safety
findings.root_cause: The ibc_app PDA, which determines which IBC application receives the packet callback, is derived from the port identifier in msg.payloads[0], the relayer-supplied metadata struct. In the recv_packet instruction, this is msg.payloads[0].dest_port (recv_packet.rs#L31),
findings.body:
[H-2] Relayer-controlled metadata port routes packets to the
              wrong IBC application, breaking core routing safety

               SEVERITY: High                                    IMPACT: High


               STATUS: Resolved                                  LIKELIHOOD: Medium




              Target
               • recv_packet.rs#L31
               • ack_packet.rs#L35
               • timeout_packet.rs#L33


              Description:
              The ibc_app PDA, which determines which IBC application receives the packet callback, is
              derived from the port identifier in msg.payloads[0], the relayer-supplied metadata struct.
              In the recv_packet instruction, this is msg.payloads[0].dest_port (recv_packet.rs#L31),

                30: #[account(
                31:     seeds = [IBCApp/:SEED, msg.payloads[0].dest_port.as_bytes()],
                32:     bump
                33: )]
                34: pub ibc_app: Account<'info, IBCApp>,


              while in ack_packet and timeout_packet the equivalent field is
              msg.payloads[0].source_port.

              When operating in inline mode (the packet carries its payloads directly inside
              msg.packet.payloads, not chunked), the handler in validate_and_reconstruct_packet (
              chunking.rs#L365-368) uses msg.packet.payloads as the authoritative payload data. The
              light client membership proof then verifies the commitment over this inline payload.
              Nothing ever checks that the port in msg.payloads[0] (metadata) matches the port in
              msg.packet.payloads[0] (verified payload). The two are entirely independent inputs.

              Exploitability hinges on inline-mode packets paired with metadata entries where
              total_chunks /= 0. In this case, the metadata is still consumed for ibc_app PDA
              derivation, but payload/commitment verification uses the inline payload.
              A relayer with RELAYER_ROLE can exploit this gap by submitting a legitimate inline packet,
              for example, a token transfer with dest_port = "transfer", while setting the metadata

 COSMOS LABS     SMART CONTRACT SECURITY ASSESSMENT                                             VERSION 1.1




              dest_port to a different registered application, such as "oracle".

              The light client verifies the actual transfer packet, but the on_recv_packet CPI goes to the
              oracle app instead of the transfer app. The receipt and acknowledgement are written
              against the verified packet, so the transfer app never receives its callback.

              The vulnerability exists across all three packet lifecycle instructions. Following is the
              concrete impact on IFT (token transfers) and GMP, which together handle cross-chain
              value movement on Solana:
               • recv_packet: IFT token minting on the destination chain happens via GMP's
                 on_recv_packet, which executes a CPI to ift_mint (on_recv_packet.rs#L198). If the
                 router sends this callback to the wrong app and that app returns a valid
                 acknowledgement, the packet receipt is written permanently and the source chain sees
                 a success ack. The correct app (GMP) never executes ift_mint, so no tokens are
                 minted on the destination. The source chain considers the transfer complete, resulting
                 in a cross-chain token loss.
               • ack_packet: GMP's on_ack_packet creates a GMPCallResultAccount (
                 on_ack_packet.rs#L64), which IFT's finalize_transfer reads to decide whether to
                 refund or complete (finalize_transfer.rs#L153). If the ack callback goes to the wrong
                 app, packet_commitment is closed (close = relayer) but GMPCallResultAccount is never
                 created. finalize_transfer becomes permanently uncallable. Consequently, the
                 PendingTransfer PDA stays alive, the sender's burned tokens are never refunded, and
                 the transfer can never complete.
               • timeout_packet: GMP's on_timeout_packet creates a GMPCallResultAccount with
                 CallResultStatus/:Timeout (on_timeout_packet.rs#L64), which triggers the refund
                 path in finalize_transfer (finalize_transfer.rs#L154-175). If misrouted, the commitment
                 is closed but no GMPCallResultAccount exists. The sender's tokens were burned in
                 ift_transfer and no refund is possible.



              Recommendations:
              Consider cross-validating the metadata port against the inline payload port before or
              during account resolution.
              For recv_packet, require that msg.payloads[0].dest_port /=
              msg.packet.payloads[0].dest_port when inline payloads are present, and apply the
              equivalent check for source_port in ack_packet and timeout_packet.
              Alternatively, derive the ibc_app PDA directly from the inline payload's port field when the
              packet carries inline payloads, removing the metadata dependency from the routing
              decision entirely.
              Cosmos Labs: Resolved with @b66d7de3f4//.

              Zenith: Verified.

 COSMOS LABS     SMART CONTRACT SECURITY ASSESSMENT                                           VERSION 1.1

findings.title: Shared ClientSequence counter causes stale PDA derivation and packet send DoS
findings.root_cause: The send_packet instruction handler reads ClientSequence.next_sequence_send at runtime to derive the expected packet commitment PDA, then checks it against the account the caller provided in the transaction's account list. On Solana, account addresses are fixed at signing time, so the caller must read the counter off-chain and derive the PDA before submitting.
findings.body:
[M-1] Shared ClientSequence counter causes stale PDA
              derivation and packet send DoS

               SEVERITY: Medium                                    IMPACT: Medium


               STATUS: Resolved                                    LIKELIHOOD: Medium




              Target
               • programs/solana/programs/ics26-router/src/instructions/send_packet.rs#L108-L121
               • programs/solana/programs/ics26-router/src/instructions/send_packet.rs#L174-L177



              Description
              The send_packet instruction handler reads ClientSequence.next_sequence_send at
              runtime to derive the expected packet commitment PDA, then checks it against the
              account the caller provided in the transaction's account list. On Solana, account addresses
              are fixed at signing time, so the caller must read the counter off-chain and derive the PDA
              before submitting.
              If any other sender on the same source_client lands first and causes the sequence
              counter to be incremented, the runtime computes a different PDA than what the caller
              supplied. The equality check in

                166: let (expected_pda, bump) = Pubkey/:find_program_address(
                167:     &[
                168:         Commitment/:PACKET_COMMITMENT_SEED,
                169:         source_client.as_bytes(),
                170:         &sequence.to_le_bytes(),
                171:     ],
                172:     &crate/:ID,
                173: );
                174: require!(
                175:     packet_commitment_info.key() /= expected_pda,
                176:     RouterError/:InvalidChunkAccount
                177: );

 COSMOS LABS     SMART CONTRACT SECURITY ASSESSMENT                                            VERSION 1.1




              fails with InvalidChunkAccount, reverting the transaction.
              Unlike most Solana programs where mutable state is scoped per-user or per-pool, here a
              single ClientSequence account is shared across all IBC applications and all senders on a
              client. Under organic high throughput, multiple legitimate senders will frequently invalidate
              each other's pre-derived PDAs without any malicious intent. This also opens the door to
              targeted griefing via transaction ordering.


              Recommendations
              Consider a per-sender sequence counter.
              Cosmos Labs: Resolved with @a10d837ce5//. Apps should be able to either receive a
              sequence number from the original caller or hash some salt to produce a random
              sequence that is very likely to be unused. The frontends could also check whether a packet
              commitment account exists before sending a sequence. Off-chain coordination is an
              accepted risk.
              Zenith: Verified.

 COSMOS LABS     SMART CONTRACT SECURITY ASSESSMENT                                           VERSION 1.1

findings.title: Pre-funded packet commitment PDA blocks send_packet for targeted senders
findings.root_cause: The send_packet instruction creates packet commitment PDAs at runtime using anchor_lang/:system_program/:create_account via CPI to the System Program. This manual path is necessary because the sequence number is computed at runtime through calculate_namespaced_sequence and cannot be expressed in Anchor's static seed derivation.
findings.body:
[M-2] Pre-funded packet commitment PDA blocks send_packet
              for targeted senders

               SEVERITY: Medium                                 IMPACT: Medium


               STATUS: Resolved                                 LIKELIHOOD: Medium




              Target
               • ics26-router/src/instructions/send_packet.rs#L191-L203


              Description
              The send_packet instruction creates packet commitment PDAs at runtime using
              anchor_lang/:system_program/:create_account via CPI to the System Program. This
              manual path is necessary because the sequence number is computed at runtime through
              calculate_namespaced_sequence and cannot be expressed in Anchor's static seed
              derivation.
              The System Program's CreateAccount instruction contains a hard precondition: the
              destination account must have zero lamports. If any lamports are already present, the
              instruction fails with AccountAlreadyInUse. Since Solana allows transferring lamports to
              any address (including off-curve PDA addresses) without requiring a signature from the
              destination, an adversary can pre-fund the target PDA to trigger this failure.
              All seed components for the packet commitment PDA are publicly derivable:
               • PACKET_COMMITMENT_SEED is a constant.
               • source_client is the IBC client identifier, visible on-chain.
               • sequence is computed as base_sequence * 10000 + sha256(app_program /| payer) %
                 10000, where base_sequence is readable from the ClientSequence account's
                 next_sequence_send field, and app_program / payer are public keys.

              An attacker reads next_sequence_send on-chain, computes the target sequence for a
              known sender, derives the PDA, and transfers 1 lamport to it. When the legitimate sender's
              send_packet transaction executes, the create_account CPI at line 191 fails, reverting the
              entire instruction. Because the revert is atomic, next_sequence_send is never incremented.
              The same sender retries with the same sequence and hits the same pre-funded PDA
              indefinitely.
              The targeted sender remains blocked until a different sender (who produces a different
              sequence suffix) successfully advances the base sequence.

 COSMOS LABS     SMART CONTRACT SECURITY ASSESSMENT                                         VERSION 1.1




              Recommendations
              Consider replacing the raw create_account CPI with the defensive pattern used internally
              by Anchor's init: when the PDA already holds lamports, transfer only the delta needed for
              rent exemption, then use allocate and assign via invoke_signed to initialize the account.
              This provides the same pre-funding resistance as init_if_needed while keeping the
              runtime-computed seed flexibility the manual path needs.
              Cosmos Labs: Resolved with @a10d837ce5//.
              Zenith: Verified.

 COSMOS LABS     SMART CONTRACT SECURITY ASSESSMENT                                              VERSION 1.1

findings.title: IFT refund mints are subject to rate limit and pause state, contrary to spec
findings.root_cause: The IFT architecture ADR (docs/adr/solana-ift-architecture.md#L214) states:
findings.body:
[M-3] IFT refund mints are subject to rate limit and pause state,
              contrary to spec

               SEVERITY: Medium                                   IMPACT: Medium


               STATUS: Acknowledged                               LIKELIHOOD: Medium




              Target
               • programs/solana/programs/ift/src/instructions/finalize_transfer.rs#L30-L38
               • programs/solana/programs/ift/src/helpers.rs#L15-L42



              Description
              The IFT architecture ADR (docs/adr/solana-ift-architecture.md#L214) states:

                "All mint paths (except refunds) respect daily rate limits and pause state."


              The implementation diverges from this intent in two ways:


              1. Rate limit: finalize_transfer() issues refund mints through mint_to_account(),
                 which unconditionally calls check_and_update_mint_rate_limit(). Refunds on timeout
                 and error ACK therefore consume daily budget just like inbound mints, while only
                 success ACK frees budget via reduce_mint_rate_limit_usage().
                 This asymmetry could be exploited to grief the refund mechanism: an attacker burns
                 tokens via ift_transfer() with a short timeout (as reported in another finding, the
                 minimum timeout is only 12 seconds, instead of the intended 60 seconds), lets the
                 packet time out, and collects a refund mint. The net token balance remains unchanged,
                 but the rate-limit budget is reduced. Repeating this exhausts the daily limit at the cost of
                 transaction fees only. Once exhausted, legitimate ift_mint calls and other users'
                 refunds revert until the next day.

              2. Pause state: Checking constraint = !app_state.paused @ IFTError/:AppPaused (
                 finalize_transfer.rs#L35) blocks all refunds while the token bridge is paused.


              Recommendations
              Consider skipping the pause check and rate limit on the timeout and error-ACK refund
              paths in finalize_transfer(). Both controls remain appropriate in the other scenarios.

 COSMOS LABS     SMART CONTRACT SECURITY ASSESSMENT                                           VERSION 1.1




              Cosmos Labs: Acknowledged. We will not address this. This is an acceptable risk to us at
              this point. In the future, we want to mitigate this with a more sophisticated rate-limiting
              logic.

 COSMOS LABS     SMART CONTRACT SECURITY ASSESSMENT                                         VERSION 1.1

findings.title: Hardcoded GMP encoding constant prevents Solana-to-EVM IFT transfers
findings.root_cause: ChainOptions/:Evm in the IFT program produces a correct ABI-encoded iftMint(address, uint256) inner payload via construct_evm_mint_call(). The GMP layer, however, hardcodes ICS27_ENCODING = "application/x-protobuf" and protobuf-encodes the GmpPacketData wrapper for every outbound packet regardless of the destination.
findings.body:
[M-4] Hardcoded GMP encoding constant prevents
              Solana-to-EVM IFT transfers

               SEVERITY: Medium                                IMPACT: Medium


               STATUS: Resolved                                LIKELIHOOD: High




              Target
               • programs/solana/programs/ics27-gmp/src/constants.rs#L14
               • programs/solana/programs/ics27-gmp/src/instructions/send_call.rs#L155
               • programs/solana/programs/ift/src/instructions/ift_transfer.rs#L249-L261



              Description:
              ChainOptions/:Evm in the IFT program produces a correct ABI-encoded iftMint(address,
              uint256) inner payload via construct_evm_mint_call(). The GMP layer, however,
              hardcodes ICS27_ENCODING = "application/x-protobuf" and protobuf-encodes the
              GmpPacketData wrapper for every outbound packet regardless of the destination.

              On the EVM side, the onRecvPacket() function
              rejects any encoding other than "application/x-solidity-abi". abi.decode() would
              revert on the protobuf-encoded wrapper.
              The ChainOptions/:Evm path is therefore broken. Tokens are burned on Solana, the packet
              is committed, but the EVM destination always rejects it and reverts. The ICS26 EVM router
              catches the revert and writes an error-ACK, so the sender on Solana can reclaim tokens via
              finalize_transfer once the error ACK is relayed back. As a result, the IFT transfers from
              Solana to EVM are effectively non-functional.


              Recommendations:
              Consider selecting the correct encoding in GMP's send_call based on the destination
              chain.
              Cosmos Labs: Resolved with @2b61dcd182//.

              Zenith: Verified.

 COSMOS LABS     SMART CONTRACT SECURITY ASSESSMENT                                            VERSION 1.1

              system_instruction/:create_account. On Solana, this instruction fails with
              AccountAlreadyInUse if the destination account already holds any lamports, even if it has
              no data and is still owned by the System Program.
              An attacker can derive the PDA, and send a dust lamport amount to it before the
              ift_transfer instruction lands, thereby griefing the victim's cross-chain IFT transfer due to
              the create_account erroring out.

              This is the same class of issue as the packet_commitment PDA prefunding vulnerability in
              send_packet.rs, reported in "Pre-funded packet commitment PDA blocks send_packet for
              targeted senders".


              Recommendations:
              Consider replacing the raw create_account CPI with the defensive pattern used internally
              by Anchor's init: when the PDA already holds lamports, transfer only the delta needed for
              rent exemption, then use allocate and assign via invoke_signed to initialize the account.
              This provides the same pre-funding resistance as init_if_needed while keeping the
              runtime-computed seed flexibility the manual path needs.

findings.title: Anchor's Borsh-wrapped return data corrupts acknowledgement bytes delivered to source chain IBC apps
findings.root_cause: Anchor's #[program] codegen Borsh-serializes the return value of every instruction handler before calling set_return_data(). For Result<Vec<u8>>, this prepends a 4-byte little-endian length prefix.
findings.body:
[M-6] Anchor's Borsh-wrapped return data corrupts
              acknowledgement bytes delivered to source chain IBC apps

               SEVERITY: Medium                                  IMPACT: Medium


               STATUS: Resolved                                  LIKELIHOOD: High




              Target
               • programs/solana/packages/solana-ibc-types/src/ibc_app.rs#L158-L162
               • programs/solana/programs/ics26-router/src/instructions/recv_packet.rs#L222-L236



              Description:
              Anchor's #[program] codegen Borsh-serializes the return value of every instruction handler
              before calling set_return_data(). For Result<Vec<u8>>, this prepends a 4-byte
              little-endian length prefix. A 7-byte ack becomes 11 bytes: 07 00 00 00 followed by the
              original 7 bytes.

              The router's CPI helper in ibc_app.rs:160 reads the return data as-is without stripping this
              Borsh envelope:

                158: // Get acknowledgement from return data
                159: match get_return_data() {
                160:     Some((program_id, data)) if program_id /= *ctx.program.key />
                    Ok(data),
                161:     _ /> err!(IbcAppError/:InvalidAppResponse),
                162: }


              The wrapped bytes propagate through the full ack pipeline: committed as sha256(0x02 /|
              sha256(borsh_wrapped_ack)), emitted in WriteAcknowledgementEvent,
              forwarded by the relayer, and delivered to the source chain's onAcknowledgementPacket.
              Commitment verification still passes because both sides hash the same wrapped bytes, but
              the source chain app receives [4_byte_len /| actual_ack] instead of actual_ack.
              This breaks the Solidity GMP app's error detection,

                171: IBCSenderCallbacksLib.ackPacketCallback(
                172:     sender, keccak256(msg_.acknowledgement) /=
                    ICS24Host.KECCAK256_UNIVERSAL_ERROR_ACK, msg_
                173: );

 COSMOS LABS     SMART CONTRACT SECURITY ASSESSMENT                                           VERSION 1.1




              The Borsh-wrapped ack never matches the precomputed hash of the raw error constant,
              so error ACKs are always misclassified as success. Any app that ABI- or protobuf-decodes
              the ack content will also fail or produce garbage.
              For comparison, the EVM side does not have this problem.
              The onRecvPacket function returns raw bytes memory with no wrapping.


              Recommendations:
              Consider Borsh-deserializing the return data in on_recv_packet to strip the length prefix
              before returning it to the router.
              Cosmos Labs: Resolved with @f63fb73681//. and @80f10aaf0b//.

              Zenith: Verified.

findings.title: No pause/unpause mechanism for router despite documented emergency roles
findings.root_cause: The RouterState account has no paused flag and the program exposes no pause or unpause instruction, despite the project's own documentation defining PAUSER_ROLE (ID 2) and UNPAUSER_ROLE (ID 3) for exactly this purpose.
findings.body:
[M-7] No pause/unpause mechanism for router despite
              documented emergency roles

               SEVERITY: Medium                                 IMPACT: High


               STATUS: Resolved                                 LIKELIHOOD: Low




              Target
               • ics26-router/src/instructions/recv_packet.rs


              Description:
              The RouterState account has no paused flag and the program exposes no pause or
              unpause instruction, despite the project's own documentation defining PAUSER_ROLE (ID 2)
              and UNPAUSER_ROLE (ID 3) for exactly this purpose.

              In the event of a security incident, such as a light client compromise, a malicious IBC app,
              or an exploit in the counterparty chain, there is no atomic mechanism to halt all IBC packet
              flow.
              The Ethereum implementation of ICS26Router includes a pause/unpause mechanism gated
              by the corresponding roles, making this a deviation from the cross-chain specification and
              a reduction in operational safety guarantees on the Solana side.


              Recommendations:
              We recommend adding a paused: bool field to the RouterState account and
              implementing two new instructions, pause gated by PAUSER_ROLE and unpause gated by
              UNPAUSER_ROLE, that toggle this flag. Each packet-processing instruction (send_packet,
              recv_packet, ack_packet, timeout_packet) should check
              require!(!router_state.paused, RouterError/:ProtocolPaused) at the top of its
              handler, before any state mutation. This provides a single-transaction emergency brake
              that immediately halts all IBC traffic regardless of the number of registered clients.
              Cosmos Labs: Resolved with @bd7cc43999//.

              Zenith: Verified.

findings.title: Over Claim Due To Uncapped Periods Passed
findings.root_cause: keeper::calculateClaimableFunds calculates and distributes funds to a recipient based on a budget, which is divided into several tranches, each with a specific period. Each tranche represents an allocation of funds that may be claimed after a certain period. periodsPassed is not capped by the remaining number of tranches ( TranchesLeft ).
findings.body:
Over Claim Due To Uncapped Periods Passed HIGH    OS-CDK-ADV-00

Description

keeper::calculateClaimableFunds calculates and distributes funds to a recipient based on a budget,
which is divided into several tranches, each with a specific period. Each tranche represents an allocation
of funds that may be claimed after a certain period. periodsPassed is not capped by the remaining
number of tranches ( TranchesLeft ). This allows the calculated coinsToDistribute to become
arbitrarily large if enough time has passed, resulting in potential overflow in TranchesLeft and exceeding
the TotalBudget .

>_ x/protocolpool/keeper/keeper.go    go
T
func (k Keeper) calculateClaimableFunds(ctx context.Context, recipient sdk.AccAddress, budget
→ types.Budget, currentTime time.Time) (amount sdk.Coin, err error) {
[...]
// Calculate how many periods have passed
periodsPassed := int64(timeElapsed) / int64(*budget.Period)
F
// Calculate the amount to distribute for all passed periods
coinsToDistribute := math.NewInt(periodsPassed).
→ Mul(budget.TotalBudget.Amount.QuoRaw(int64(budget.Tranches)))
amount = sdk.NewCoin(budget.TotalBudget.Denom, coinsToDistribute)

//Update the budget's remaining tranches
budget.TranchesLeft -= uint64(periodsPassed)
A
// update the ClaimedAmount
claimedAmount := budget.ClaimedAmount.Add(amount)
budget.ClaimedAmount = &claimedAmount
[...]
return amount, nil
R
}

Thus, since claimedAmount is updated without checking if it exceeds TotalBudget , the recipient
may effectively claim more funds than allocated in the budget, given enough time has passed since the
last claim, resulting in an overclaim.
D

Remediation

Ensure that the calculation of periodsPassed is capped by TranchesLeft .

Patch

Resolved in 03d70aa.

findings.title: Premature Fund Claim
findings.root_cause: The vulnerability in keeper::calculateClaimableFunds arises from the incorrect update of the NextClaimFrom field, which tracks the time from which the next claim may be made. This miscalculation allows users to prematurely claim funds that are intended for future periods.
findings.body:
Premature Fund Claim HIGH    OS-CDK-ADV-01

Description

The vulnerability in keeper::calculateClaimableFunds arises from the incorrect update of the
NextClaimFrom field, which tracks the time from which the next claim may be made. This miscalculation
allows users to prematurely claim funds that are intended for future periods. In the current implementation,
NextClaimFrom is updated by adding a single period to the previous NextClaimFrom value rather
than accounting for the actual number of periods that have passed.

>_ x/protocolpool/keeper/keeper.go    go
func (k Keeper) calculateClaimableFunds(ctx context.Context, recipient sdk.AccAddress, budget
T
→ types.Budget, currentTime time.Time) (amount sdk.Coin, err error) {
[...]
// update the ClaimedAmount
claimedAmount := budget.ClaimedAmount.Add(amount)
budget.ClaimedAmount = &claimedAmount
F
// Update the last claim time for the budget
nextClaimFrom := budget.NextClaimFrom.Add(*budget.Period)
budget.NextClaimFrom = &nextClaimFrom

[...]
return amount, nil
}    A

As a result, the user may claim funds for periods that have not yet elapsed. A recipient may exploit this
vulnerability by repeatedly calling the calculateClaimableFunds and prematurely claiming funds.
R

Remediation

Update NextClaimFrom by adding the total elapsed periods ( Period*periodsPassed ) to the last
claim time.
D

Patch

Resolved in 03d70aa.

findings.title: Potential To Rotate Consensus Key Back To Initial Key
findings.root_cause: The vulnerability arises from the omission of the initial consensus key from the NewToOldConsKeyMap in msg_server::RotateConsPubKey . NewToOldConsKeyMap is utilized to track historical rotations of the consensus public key ( ConsensusPubKey ) for validators.
findings.body:
Potential To Rotate Consensus Key Back To Initial Key MEDIUM    OS-CDK-ADV-02

Description

The vulnerability arises from the omission of the initial consensus key from the NewToOldConsKeyMap
in msg_server::RotateConsPubKey . NewToOldConsKeyMap is utilized to track historical rotations
of the consensus public key ( ConsensusPubKey ) for validators. Before rotating to a new public key
( NewPubkey ), the function checks if this new key is already present in NewToOldConsKeyMap . If
the NewToOldConsKeyMap does not include the initial (first) consensus key of a validator, it allows the
possibility of rotating back to the validator’s very first consensus key.

>_ x/staking/keeper/msg_server.go    go
T
func (k msgServer) RotateConsPubKey(ctx context.Context, msg *types.MsgRotateConsPubKey) (res
→ *types.MsgRotateConsPubKeyResponse, err error) {
[...]
// check cons key is already present in the key rotation history.
rotatedTo, err := k.NewToOldConsKeyMap.Get(ctx, pk.Address())
F
if err != nil && !errors.Is(err, collections.ErrNotFound) {
return nil, err
}
if rotatedTo != nil {
return nil, errorsmod.Wrap(sdkerrors.ErrInvalidAddress,
"the new public key is already present in rotation history, please try with
→ a different one")
A
}
[...]
}

Consensus key rotation is designed to enhance security by periodically changing keys. Allowing rotation
R
back to the initial key defeats this purpose, as compromised keys may be utilized again. Additionally,
RotateConsPubKey does not validate whether the new consensus key conforms to the allowed key
types defined by the network’s consensus parameters. Validators may end up with consensus keys of
different types, which may not be supported by the protocol.

D
Remediation

Update RotateConsPubKey to include the initial consensus key in the NewToOldConsKeyMap or
maintain a separate mechanism to track the initial key separately. Additionally, include a validation step to
ensure that the new consensus key type matches one of the allowed key types specified in the consensus
parameters.

findings.title: Same-timestamp staking injects post-snapshot voting power
findings.root_cause: A proposal snapshots totalVotingPower and block.timestamp before returning. Staking checkpoints use the same timestamp and votingPowerAt() accepts the last checkpoint whose timestamp is less than or equal to the proposal timestamp.
findings.body:
[C-1] Same-timestamp staking injects post-snapshot voting
             power

               SEVERITY: Critical                                   IMPACT: High


               STATUS: Resolved                                     LIKELIHOOD: High




             Target
              • DaimonGovernor.sol


             Description:
             A proposal snapshots totalVotingPower and block.timestamp before returning. Staking
             checkpoints use the same timestamp and votingPowerAt() accepts the last checkpoint
             whose timestamp is less than or equal to the proposal timestamp.

             Consequently, voting power acquired after propose() but later in the same transaction or
             block is:
              • absent from snapshotTotalVotingPower, but
              • included in the attacker's votingPowerAt(attacker, snapshotTimestamp).

             The same-timestamp checkpoint logic either creates a checkpoint at the proposal times-
             tamp or overwrites an existing checkpoint at that timestamp. Transaction ordering—not
             merely block ordering—is therefore erased.
             This can be exploited atomically through a coordinator contract, it does not require reacting
             to an already-mined proposal or controlling a validator. An attacker can introduce voting
             weight after seeing and creating the proposal while omitting that weight from the quorum
             denominator. If the injected weight clears quorum and exceeds opposing votes, the attacker
             can pass an arbitrary Timelock action, including a UUPS upgrade capable of taking control
             of the full token state.
             Under current defaults, one maximum-size 365-day stake grants:
              • 5 billion DMN × 4 = 20 billion voting-power units.

             Multiple stakes can be included in the same transaction or block, bounded by the attacker's






             liquid balance and block gas. The maximum default theoretical injected weight is approxi-
             mately four times the liquid supply.
             The attack still requires real DMN to be locked and retains the normal voting and Timelock
             periods, but it defeats the protocol's central promise that power obtained after proposal
             creation cannot affect that proposal.


             Proof of Concept:

               function test_PoC_sameBlockStakeBypassesSnapshot() public {
                   address attacker = address(0xBAD);

                   _stake(address(0xBEEF), 99_000 ether, 0);
                   _stake(attacker, 1_000 ether, 0); // enough to propose
                   fundWithDmn(attacker, 9_000 ether);
                   assertEq(staking.totalVotingPower(), 100_000 ether);


                   vm.startPrank(attacker);
                   token.approve(address(staking), 9_000 ether);
                   uint256 id = governor.propose(address(token), 0, "", "p");
                   uint256 snapshot = block.timestamp;
                   staking.stake(9_000 ether, 0); // no warp: checkpoint is written at the
                   snapshot
                   vm.stopPrank();

                   assertEq(staking.votingPowerAt(attacker, snapshot), 10_000 ether);
                   assertEq(staking.totalVotingPower(), 109_000 ether); // consistent quorum:
                    10,900 VP


                   vm.warp(snapshot + governor.VOTING_DELAY());
                   vm.prank(attacker);
                   governor.castVote(id, 1);

                   vm.warp(snapshot + governor.VOTING_DELAY() + governor.VOTING_PERIOD() + 1)
                   ;
                   assertEq(_state(id), SUCCEEDED); // passes against the stale 10,000 VP
                   quorum
               }




             Recommendations:
             Use checkpoints with ordering granularity that cannot be modified after the snapshot. Pre-
             fer block-number checkpoints for both per-account and aggregate voting power. When
             creating a proposal:






              • set the snapshot to the last completed block, block.number - 1
              • obtain voter weights from votingPowerAt(account, snapshotBlock)
              • obtain the quorum denominator from totalVotingPowerAt(snapshotBlock)

             If timestamp checkpoints are retained, using block.timestamp - 1 prevents the specific
             post-proposal staking injection because subsequent checkpoints cannot affect that past
             timepoint. However, BSC can produce several adjacent blocks with the same whole-second
             timestamp, so this represents the previous second rather than precisely the previous block
             and may exclude legitimate voting-power changes from earlier blocks in the current second.
             Daimon DAO: Resolved with @e029db0//. — voting power checkpoints now keyed by block
             number rather than timestamp, and the proposal snapshot is taken at block.number - 1.
             Zenith: Verified.






             4.2 High Risk
             A total of 1 high risk findings were identified.

findings.title: Mutable quorum retroactively changes completed pro- posal outcomes
findings.root_cause: The Governor snapshots total voting power when a proposal is created, but does not snap- shot the applicable quorum percentage. Instead, state() evaluates every completed pro- posal using the current global quorumBps.
findings.body:
[H-1] Mutable quorum retroactively changes completed pro-
             posal outcomes

               SEVERITY: High                                   IMPACT: High


               STATUS: Resolved                                 LIKELIHOOD: Medium




             Target
              • src/DaimonGovernor.sol#L124-L138
              • src/DaimonGovernor.sol#L164-L205
              • src/DaimonGovernor.sol#L227-L233


             Description:
             The Governor snapshots total voting power when a proposal is created, but does not snap-
             shot the applicable quorum percentage. Instead, state() evaluates every completed pro-
             posal using the current global quorumBps.

               uint256 quorumNeeded =
                    (p.snapshotTotalVotingPower * quorumBps) / 10000;


             Consequently, changing quorumBps retroactively changes proposal outcomes. A proposal
             defeated solely for insufficient quorum can become Succeeded after quorum is lowered.
             Because unqueued proposals do not expire, anyone can subsequently queue the revived
             proposal and execute it after the Timelock delay.

             Raising quorum causes the inverse failure. It can turn a successful or already queued pro-
             posal into Defeated. Although queue() sets p.queued, state() does not preserve a queued
             state and continues recalculating the result. execute() then requires the dynamically evalu-
             ated state to remain Succeeded, potentially stranding an operation already scheduled in the
             Timelock.

             The provided deployment script initializes quorum at the 10% minimum. Revival therefore
             requires a reachable sequence such as raising quorum to 20%, creating a proposal that fails
             only under that threshold, and later lowering quorum to 10%. Raising quorum can affect

 DAIMON DAO   SMART CONTRACT SECURITY ASSESSMENT                                             VERSION 1.1




             historical proposals on the first adjustment.
             This does not bypass voting, queueing, or the seven-day Timelock. However, it breaks
             vote-outcome finality and can make an action rejected under its contemporaneous rules
             executable. Proposals support arbitrary targets, values, and calldata, so a revived proposal
             can perform governance-controlled upgrades, role or parameter changes, or transfers of
             Timelock funds. Guardian cancellation and the Timelock reaction window mitigate the risk
             but require continuous monitoring and do not prevent successful queued proposals from
             becoming non-executable.


             Recommendations:
             It is recommended to snapshot quorumBps for every proposal at creation and exclusively use
             that stored value when evaluating its outcome.

               struct Proposal {
                   // ...
                   uint256 quorumBpsSnapshot;
               }

               p.quorumBpsSnapshot = quorumBps;


               uint256 quorumNeeded =
                   (p.snapshotTotalVotingPower * p.quorumBpsSnapshot) / 10000;


             Alternatively, checkpoint quorum changes and query the value applicable to the proposal’s
             snapshot, with same-timepoint behavior explicitly defined.

             Add tests confirming that:
              • lowering quorum does not revive defeated proposals;
              • raising quorum does not defeat successful proposals;
              • queued proposals remain executable after quorum changes; and
              • newly created proposals use the updated quorum.

             DaimonGovernor is not upgradeable. Existing deployments therefore require Governor re-
             placement and Timelock role rewiring; the correction should be included before mainnet
             deployment.
             Daimon DAO: Resolved with @e029db0//.
             Zenith: Verified.

findings.title: Automatic fee sales can under-mint liquidity additions
findings.root_cause: DaimonV2._transfer() treats every transfer to uniswapV2Pair as a sale. This includes the token transfer performed by PancakeSwap's addLiquidityETH().
findings.body:
[M-1] Automatic fee sales can under-mint liquidity additions

              SEVERITY: Medium                                    IMPACT: High


              STATUS: Resolved                                    LIKELIHOOD: Low




             Target
              • DaimonV2.sol


             Description:
             DaimonV2._transfer() treats every transfer to uniswapV2Pair as a sale. This includes the
             token transfer performed by PancakeSwap's addLiquidityETH(). If the Daimon contract
             holds at least minimumTokensBeforeSwap, _transfer() calls _swapAccumulatedFees() before
             crediting the liquidity provider's tokens to the pair.
             At that point, the router has already read the pair reserves, selected the token and BNB
             contribution amounts, and performed the applicable checks governed by amountTokenMin
             and amountETHMin. Selling the accumulated DMN increases the pair's DMN balance and
             reserve while decreasing its WBNB balance and reserve. Any subsequent buyback also
             changes the same reserves. The contribution amounts calculated by the router are therefore
             stale when the outer liquidity addition resumes.
             The full sequence is:
              • addLiquidityETH() reads the current reserves, calculates the proportional contribution,
                and checks the applicable minimum amounts.
              • The router transfers DMN to the pair, which enters DaimonV2._transfer() and triggers
                _swapAccumulatedFees().
              • The nested sale adds DMN to the pair, removes WBNB, and updates the pair reserves
                before the liquidity provider's transfer is applied.
              • The outer transfer completes and the router deposits the WBNB amount calculated from
                the earlier reserve ratio without reading the reserves again.
              • The pair's mint() calculates LP shares from the smaller of the two proportional balance
                increases. After a net DMN sale, the DMN side limits the minted shares and part of the
                WBNB contribution mints no LP shares.






              • mint() then updates the reserves to the pair's complete balances, including the entire
                WBNB deposit. The unmatched WBNB becomes pool backing shared with incumbent
                LP holders.
             The configured router minimums do not protect the liquidity provider. They constrain the
             contribution amounts selected from the reserve snapshot before the token callback. They
             do not enforce the reserve ratio after the transfers or a minimum amount of LP tokens, so
             the nested reserve change does not cause the liquidity addition to revert.
             This condition can occur accidentally when organically accumulated fees reach the thresh-
             old and the next transfer to the pair is a liquidity addition. It can also be induced intentionally,
             although this is less likely because profitable exploitation requires a material incumbent LP
             position, a sufficiently large pending liquidity addition, and transaction ordering. Such a
             party can top up the Daimon contract to the swap threshold immediately before the liq-
             uidity addition, then withdraw its incumbent LP position after the under-minted deposit has
             increased the backing of its shares.


             Recommendations:
             Do not execute fee sales or buybacks synchronously from transfers to the AMM pair. Move
             fee processing to a separate permissionless operation so it completes before the router
             reads reserves. If the existing transfer behavior must remain, use a liquidity integration that
             revalidates the post-callback reserve ratio and enforces a minimum LP token output.
             Daimon DAO: Resolved with @043d8b6//. (PR 25) — automation is skipped when
             msg.sender is the configured router. Third leg of the plan, alongside #27's isolation and
             #28's per-block budgets.
             One consequence worth flagging, since it changes a property we stated in scoping. Ordi-
             nary sells also reach _transfer through the router, so they no longer trigger fee conversion
             either. Conversion now depends on a direct transfer to the pair — permissionless, one wei
             is enough, bounded by the #28 budgets, but a liveness dependency the protocol didn't
             have before.
             We verified against the canonical periphery before accepting this rather than assuming it.
             Sells were never exposed to the staleness in #1: in the fee-supporting variant the output is
             computed after the token callback and amountOutMin is checked against what actually ar-
             rives. Liquidity additions differ in kind — their minimums are consumed before the callback
             and mint() has no minimum output at all, which is the whole finding.

             But the callee cannot distinguish them: at the token leg both are byte-identical transfer-
             From(holder → pair) with msg.sender == router, and the EVM gives no introspection into
             the caller's frame. The obvious heuristic — probing for a WBNB surplus on the pair — fails
             because addLiquidityETH transfers the token before depositing WETH, so the surplus is zero
             exactly when it would matter.

             On the sell side the skip is an improvement, not a cost: sellers no longer pay the automa-
             tion's gas inside their own transaction, nor have their slippage budget consumed by a swap






             guaranteed to land immediately before theirs.
             Documented in THREAT_MODEL §8 with the reasoning, and in the mainnet checklist as an
             operational item.
             Zenith: Verified. The change correctly prevents fee swaps and buybacks during liquidity
             additions through the configured PancakeSwap V2 router. Third-party routers or custom
             liquidity integrations that transfer DMN directly to the pair remain exposed to the original
             stale-reserve behavior and should be treated as unsupported. Router-mediated sells also
             no longer trigger fee processing, so conversion cadence now depends on permissionless
             direct-to-pair transfers, as indicated by the Daimon team.

findings.title: Dust transfers bypass aggregate automation pacing
findings.root_cause: DaimonV2 allows transfers into uniswapV2Pair to trigger automated fee-token sales and BNB-funded buybacks. The limits applied to these operations constrain only one call; no aggregate per-block or per-epoch pacing exists.
findings.body:
[M-3] Dust transfers bypass aggregate automation pacing

              SEVERITY: Medium                                 IMPACT: Medium


              STATUS: Resolved                                 LIKELIHOOD: Medium




             Target
              • src/DaimonV2.sol#L355-L385
              • src/DaimonV2.sol#L459-L485
              • src/DaimonV2.sol#L511-L545


             Description:
             DaimonV2 allows transfers into uniswapV2Pair to trigger automated fee-token sales and
             BNB-funded buybacks. The limits applied to these operations constrain only one call; no
             aggregate per-block or per-epoch pacing exists.
             Automation executes before the triggering transfer is applied:

               if (
                   !_inSwap &&
                   swapAndLiquifyEnabled &&
                   to == uniswapV2Pair &&
                     overMin
               ) {
                     _swapAccumulatedFees(
                         minimumTokensBeforeSwap
                     );
               }


               if (
                   !_inSwap &&
                   buyBackEnabled &&
                   to == uniswapV2Pair
               ) {
                     uint256 ethBalance = address(this).balance;
                     if (
                         ethBalance > 1 ether &&
                         _tTotal > MIN_SUPPLY
                     ) {
                         uint256 spendAmount =






                             ethBalance > buyBackUpperLimit
                                 ? buyBackUpperLimit
                                 : ethBalance;

                        _buyBackAndBurn(spendAmount / 20);
                   }
               }


             The triggering transfer needs only a positive amount. At one token wei, all percentage fees
             round to zero:

               uint256 tFee =
                   (1 * taxFee) / 1000; // 0

               uint256 tLiquidity =
                   (1 * liquidityFee) / 1000; // 0


             An attacker contract can repeatedly call:

               token.transfer(uniswapV2Pair, 1);


             Each iteration costs one DMN wei plus gas. lockSwap and nonReentrant prevent nested
             execution during an individual internal operation, but they reset afterward and do not restrict
             sequential calls.
             When fee-sale automation is enabled and sufficient inventory exists, each successful itera-
             tion sells another minimumTokensBeforeSwap chunk. Repetition can process every full chunk
             in one transaction or block, leaving only a residual balance below the threshold.
             When buybacks are enabled, BNB exceeds one ether, and supply remains above
             MIN_SUPPLY, each successful iteration executes another buyback slice. Repetition can con-
             tinue until the pre-call BNB balance no longer exceeds one ether; the final buyback may
             leave slightly less than one ether.
             Consequently, minimumTokensBeforeSwap, buyBackUpperLimit, and the 5% per-call buy-
             back fraction do not limit aggregate execution. An unprivileged dust-funded actor can
             choose when the protocol realizes multiple fee-token chunks and spends most eligible buy-
             back inventory.
             The automated trades use quotes derived from the pair’s current reserves. An attacker can
             combine reserve manipulation with repeated triggers to expose multiple protocol orders
             to adversarial pricing before reversing the manipulation. Fee sales and buybacks trade in
             opposite directions, so the attacker must target the branch with material inventory, exploit
             net order flow, or adjust reserves between iterations.
             The sequence requires enabled automation, available inventory, a functioning pair, and suc-
             cessful external operations. Failed swaps do not consume the corresponding token or BNB






             inventory.


             Recommendations:
             It is recommended to enforce caller-independent aggregate limits for automated token sales
             and BNB spending.

             Track separate per-block or short-epoch budgets for:
              • cumulative DMN sold;
              • cumulative BNB spent;
              • fee-sale attempts; and
              • buyback attempts.

               if (automationBlock != block.number) {
                   automationBlock = block.number;
                   tokensSoldThisBlock = 0;
                   bnbSpentThisBlock = 0;
                   feeSwapAttemptedThisBlock = false;
                   buybackAttemptedThisBlock = false;
               }


             Consume a short-lived attempt allowance before external interaction so a caller cannot retry
             caught failures indefinitely in the same block. Refactor the automation functions to report
             success and actual execution amounts, then count only successful sales and expenditure
             against longer-lived aggregate budgets.
             Keep fee-sale and buyback budgets independent. Enforce governance-bounded maximum
             values so governance cannot accidentally configure the limits as ineffective.

             A meaningful minimum triggering amount and separate cooldowns are useful defense in
             depth but cannot replace aggregate limits because larger triggering transfers remain re-
             peatable.
             Use an independent TWAP or robust oracle with staleness and deviation checks for au-
             tomated trade validation. Aggregate pacing limits exposure but do not make same-block
             reserve quotes manipulation-resistant.

             Add PancakeSwap-compatible integration tests covering repeated dust triggers, multiple
             inventory chunks, fee sales, buybacks, caught failures, reserve manipulation, and budget
             resets.
             Daimon DAO: Resolved with @f42a629e22//.

             Zenith: Verified.

findings.title: Reflections accrued by the AMM pair can be permission- lessly skimmed
findings.root_cause: DaimonV2 excludes only deadAddress from reflection accounting. The PancakeSwap pair is created during initialization but remains reflection-included.
findings.body:
[M-4] Reflections accrued by the AMM pair can be permission-
             lessly skimmed

              SEVERITY: Medium                               IMPACT: Medium


              STATUS: Resolved                               LIKELIHOOD: Medium




             Target
             • src/DaimonV2.sol#L244-L257
             • src/DaimonV2.sol#L327-L349
             • src/DaimonV2.sol#L388-L435


             Description:
             DaimonV2 excludes only deadAddress from reflection accounting. The PancakeSwap pair
             is created during initialization but remains reflection-included.

               _isExcludedFromReward[deadAddress] = true;
               _excluded.push(deadAddress);


               uniswapV2Pair =
                   IUniswapV2Factory(uniswapV2Router.factory())
                       .createPair(
                           address(this),
                           uniswapV2Router.WETH()
                       );


             Each reflection fee reduces _rTotal, lowering the reflected-unit conversion rate and in-
             creasing the token-denominated balance of every reflection-included holder.

               function _reflectFee(
                   uint256 rFee,
                   uint256 tFee
               )
                   private
               {
                   _rTotal −= rFee;
                   _tFeeTotal += tFee;
               }






             When an unrelated taxed transfer occurs between pair reserve updates, the pair’s DMN
             balance increases passively while its recorded reserve remains unchanged:

               balanceOf(pair) > recordedReserve


             PancakeSwap V2 exposes permissionless skim(to), which transfers this balance-over-
             reserve excess to an arbitrary recipient. An unprivileged bot can therefore extract the re-
             flected excess before a swap, sync(), or liquidity operation incorporates it into the pool.
             The transfer from the pair is taxed, so the caller receives the excess net of fees. It is also
             subject to maxTxAmount; if the entire excess exceeds that limit, skim() reverts because it
             cannot request a partial amount. This is only a timing constraint because bots can monitor
             and harvest smaller profitable excesses before the limit is reached. The skim transfer’s own
             reflection can leave a smaller new excess, but this does not create an amplification loop that
             drains recorded reserves.
             The issue does not directly remove recorded AMM reserves. It diverts passive reflection
             value held by the LP-backed pair that could otherwise benefit liquidity providers through
             synchronization or balance-based liquidity removal.
             The extractable value depends on the reflection fee, organic taxed transfer volume, the pair’s
             share of reflection-included supply, reserve-update timing, transfer fees, and gas costs.
             An attacker generally cannot profitably create unlimited excess alone because generating
             reflections costs the full transfer fee while the pair receives only its proportional reflection
             share.


             Recommendations:
             It is recommended to add the pair to the fixed reflection-excluded set immediately after pair
             creation and before adding liquidity.

               uniswapV2Pair =
                   IUniswapV2Factory(uniswapV2Router.factory())
                       .createPair(
                           address(this),
                           uniswapV2Router.WETH()
                       );


               _isExcludedFromReward[uniswapV2Pair] = true;
               _excluded.push(uniswapV2Pair);


             Because a newly created pair has a zero token balance, no reflected-balance conversion is
             required.

             For an already funded pair, implement a one-time UUPS upgrade migration that atomically:






             1. reads balanceOf(pair) while the pair remains reflection-included;
             2. writes that balance to _tOwned[pair];
             3. marks the pair as reflection-excluded;

             4. registers it in _excluded exactly once; and
             5. reconciles existing balance-over-reserve excess through an explicit policy, such as an
                atomic sync() after exclusion.


               uint256 pairBalance = balanceOf(pair);


               _tOwned[pair] = pairBalance;
               _isExcludedFromReward[pair] = true;
               _excluded.push(pair);


             The existing excess must be handled separately because exclusion prevents future accrual
             but does not itself update AMM reserves.
             Do not introduce a general runtime reflection-exclusion setter. A fixed initialization or one-
             time migration preserves the project’s intended immutable exclusion model and avoids mu-
             table RFI bookkeeping risks.
             If the pair must remain reflection-included, redesign reflection allocation or explicitly doc-
             ument and accept that pair reflection is public MEV. Periodic sync() alone is not reliable
             because it can be front-run by skim() and changes pool reserves and price.
             Add PancakeSwap-compatible integration tests covering passive reflection accrual, bal-
             ance/reserve drift, skim(), transfer fees, maxTxAmount, and post-migration reserve reconcil-
             iation.

             Daimon DAO: Resolved with @ed656e7//. — the pair is added to the fixed reflection exclu-
             sion set immediately after createPair() in initialize().
             Zenith: Verified.
