findings.title: Incorrect User Index Initialization Using Static Function [RESOLVED]
findings.root_cause: The _initializeUserIndexIfNeeded() function uses REWARDS.getRewardIndex() which returns a static value that may not reflect the correct current index, causing users to miss rewards or receive incorrect reward calculations.
findings.impact: If users consistently receive more rewards than entitled due to low starting indices, the reward pool may become insolvent.
findings.body:
Issue H-1: Incorrect User Index Initialization Using
Static Function [RESOLVED]
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2026-02-kaskad-feb-16th-2026/issues/26


Summary
The _initializeUserIndexIfNeeded() function uses REWARDS.getRewardIndex() which
returns a static value that may not reflect the correct current index, causing users to
miss rewards or receive incorrect reward calculations.


Vulnerability Detail
When initializing user rewards tracking, the function captures the reward index using a
getter function:

 ur.userIndex = uint128(REWARDS.getRewardIndex(asset, reward));

 ...

       function getRewardIndex(
           address asset,
           address reward
       ) external view returns (uint256) {
           return _assets[asset].rewards[reward].index;
       }

If getRewardIndex() returns a cached or stale value rather than the dynamically
calculated current index, the userIndex will be incorrect. When rewards are later
calculated using the formula (endIndex - userIndex), users may receive more rewards
than entitled


Impact
If users consistently receive more rewards than entitled due to low starting indices, the
reward pool may become insolvent.


Tool Used
Manual Review

 Recommendation
Ensure the reward index is properly updated before capturing it for user initialization.


Discussion
KaiReytsu
Fixed. The call ordering in handleAction() ensures the user index is captured before the
snapshot updates the global index. _initializeUserIndexIfNeeded() runs first, recording
the current rewardIndex via getRewardIndex(). Only then does _maybeSnapshotPreviousEp
och() update the global index. This guarantees that (snapshotIndex - userIndex) > 0
when claiming, and the user accrues only rewards earned after their first interaction.

 // 1. Initialize user index FIRST
 _initializeUserIndexIfNeeded(user, asset, currentEpoch);
 // 2. Snapshot previous epoch (updates global index)
 _maybeSnapshotPreviousEpoch(asset, currentEpoch, totalSupply);

DemoreXTess
Index initialization is not correct. _initializeUserIndexIfNeeded calls getRewardIndex
function of rewards controller. This function is always provide stale and cached index.

 function getRewardIndex(
     address asset,
     address reward
 ) external view returns (uint256) {
     return _assets[asset].rewards[reward].index;
 }

When user is eligible to start earning rewards, this index will be used and user will earn
more rewards than expected amount.

findings.title: New Rewards Not Distributed to Existing Token Holders [ACKNOWLEDGED]
findings.root_cause: When a new reward token is added to an asset after users have already deposited, those existing users will not receive the new reward because their UserRewards struct is never initialized for the new reward.
findings.impact: Existing depositors will never receive newly added reward tokens, even though they are eligible based on their position.
findings.body:
Issue H-2: New Rewards Not Distributed to Existing
Token Holders [ACKNOWLEDGED]
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2026-02-kaskad-feb-16th-2026/issues/27
This issue has been acknowledged by the team but won't be fixed at this time.


Summary
When a new reward token is added to an asset after users have already deposited, those
existing users will not receive the new reward because their UserRewards struct is never
initialized for the new reward.


Vulnerability Detail
The _processAssetRewards() function iterates through available rewards and processes
them:
 for (uint128 r = 0; r < numRewards; ++r) {
     address reward = REWARDS.getAssetReward(ctx.asset, r);
     UserRewards storage ur = _userRewards[ctx.user][ctx.asset][reward];

     // Skip if never initialized or already processed
     if (!ur.initialized || ur.lastClaimedEpoch >= ctx.currentEpoch)
         continue;

User reward tracking is only initialized in _initializeUserIndexIfNeeded(), which is called
during handleAction(). If a user deposited before a new reward was added, their
UserRewards for that new reward will have initialized = false, causing all reward
processing to be skipped.


Impact
Existing depositors will never receive newly added reward tokens, even though they are
eligible based on their position.


Tool Used
Manual Review


Recommendation
Implement a mechanism to initialize reward tracking for existing users when new rewards
are added.

 Discussion
KaiReytsu
Acknowledged. This is a standard lazy-initialization pattern, same as Aave's
RewardsController. ERC20 provides no getHolders(), so mass-initializing all existing users
when a new reward is added is not feasible without a holder registry (which would add
gas overhead to every transfer). When a user next interacts, _initializeUserIndexIfNeed
ed iterates over all current rewards, including newly added ones, and initializes any that
are missing. The user starts accruing the new reward from their first interaction after it is
added. No previously earned rewards are lost since userIndex is set to the current global
index and the delta starts at zero.

findings.title: Epoch Snapshot Timing Causes Reward Insolvency [RESOLVED]
findings.root_cause: The reward index snapshot mechanism can capture additional rewards beyond what was allocated for an epoch if triggered after the official epoch finalization, leading to protocol insolvency where some users cannot claim their entitled rewards.
findings.impact: The recorded index includes rewards beyond what was distributed for the epoch. When all users try to claim based on this inflated index, the total claims will exceed available tokens.
findings.body:
Issue H-3: Epoch Snapshot Timing Causes Reward
Insolvency [RESOLVED]
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2026-02-kaskad-feb-16th-2026/issues/28


Summary
The reward index snapshot mechanism can capture additional rewards beyond what was
allocated for an epoch if triggered after the official epoch finalization, leading to
protocol insolvency where some users cannot claim their entitled rewards.


Vulnerability Detail
The _snapshotEpoch() function calls updateRewardIndexForTracker() to capture the
current reward index:
 uint256 index = REWARDS.updateRewardIndexForTracker(
     asset,
     reward,
     actualTotalSupply
 );

The KaskadRewardsController operates on a reward-rate-per-second basis while official
epoch handling works monthly based. If the snapshot is triggered one hour after the
official epoch end, the index will include an additional hour's worth of rewards that were
not allocated for that epoch.


Impact
The recorded index includes rewards beyond what was distributed for the epoch. When
all users try to claim based on this inflated index, the total claims will exceed available
tokens.


Tool Used
Manual Review


Recommendation
Implement a time-bounded index calculation that only accounts for rewards up to the
official epoch end timestamp.

 Discussion
KaiReytsu
Fixed. Fix details in https://github.com/Kaskad-Lending/kaskad-squashed/pull/5

findings.title: Update to entryTime when calling stake() can circumvented [RESOLVED]
findings.root_cause: StKSKDVault::_update() does not dilute the receiver's entryTime when they already have a non-zero entry, allowing users to bypass the weighted-average time dilution enforced by stake() by transferring shares from a fresh wallet.
findings.impact: Users can accumulate arbitrary additional stKSKD shares on an account without any reduction in holdingDuration(). This inflates their voting power beyond what the time-weighted mechanism intends to allow, undermining the fairness of any governance or reward system that relies on holdingDuration().
findings.body:
Issue H-4: Update to entryTime when calling stake()
can circumvented [RESOLVED]
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2026-02-kaskad-feb-16th-2026/issues/34


Summary
StKSKDVault::_update() does not dilute the receiver's entryTime when they already have
a non-zero entry, allowing users to bypass the weighted-average time dilution enforced
by stake() by transferring shares from a fresh wallet.


Vulnerability Detail
When a user calls stake(), the contract applies a weighted-average calculation to move
their entryTime forward, reducing their accumulated holdingDuration():

 // Weighted average entry time
 if (oldShares == 0) {
     entryTime[msg.sender] = uint64(block.timestamp);
 } else {
     uint64 oldEntry = entryTime[msg.sender];
     uint64 newEntry = uint64(
         (uint256(oldEntry) * oldShares + block.timestamp * shares) /
             (oldShares + shares)
     );
     entryTime[msg.sender] = newEntry;
 }

However, in _update(), when shares are transferred to a recipient who already has a
non-zero entryTime, no dilution is applied:

 // Only initialize entryTime for new recipients
 if (entryTime[to] == 0) {
     entryTime[to] = uint64(block.timestamp);
 }
 // If entryTime[to] != 0, keep their existing accumulated time

This creates an inconsistency that can be exploited:
   1. Attacker has a main account with old entryTime (high holdingDuration = high voting
      power).
  2. Attacker stakes new KSKD on a fresh wallet via stake().
  3. Fresh wallet transfers all shares to the main account.

   4. Main account receives additional shares without any entryTime dilution — its holdi
     ngDuration() remains unchanged.
If the attacker had instead called stake() directly on the main account, the
weighted-average would have moved entryTime forward, reducing their holdingDuration
() and voting power.


Impact
Users can accumulate arbitrary additional stKSKD shares on an account without any
reduction in holdingDuration(). This inflates their voting power beyond what the
time-weighted mechanism intends to allow, undermining the fairness of any governance
or reward system that relies on holdingDuration().


Recommendation
Presumable this was removed before because other users could force updates on any
receiver by transferring shares to them.
Removing this opens up this new attack vector where we can completely circumvent the
update to the entryTime when increasing our staking position.
Given that the new entryTime is scaled based on the 'amount' transferred an attacker
would have to send a significant amount to another user to alter their entryTime. This
would be in the interest of the receiver as they receive valuable assets.
If you wish to mitigate the above completely you could allow users to completely block
transfers to them by setting a flag in their account.


Discussion
KaiReytsu
Fixed. Fix details in https://github.com/Kaskad-Lending/kaskad-squashed/pull/7

findings.title: Undistributed rewards are never distributed and are instead locked in the contract. [RESOLVED]
findings.root_cause: Recycled undistributed rewards are accounted in recycledForEpoch for the next epoch but never actually added to that epoch's reward budget, permanently locking the tokens in the KaskadRewardsController contract.
findings.impact: The toNextEpoch portion of undistributed rewards (determined by undistributedToNextEp ochBps) is neither burned nor redistributed, it remains locked in the KaskadRewardsControl ler contract.
findings.body:
Issue H-5: Undistributed rewards are never distributed
and are instead locked in the contract. [RESOLVED]
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2026-02-kaskad-feb-16th-2026/issues/35


Summary
Recycled undistributed rewards are accounted in recycledForEpoch for the next epoch
but never actually added to that epoch's reward budget, permanently locking the
tokens in the KaskadRewardsController contract.


Vulnerability Detail
When ineligible users' rewards are processed, the amounts are recorded as undistributed
via recordUndistributed(). When an epoch ends, these undistributed rewards are
recycled, a portion is burned, and the remainder is earmarked for the next epoch:
https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2026-02-kaskad-feb-16th-2026/blob/main/kaskad-
squashed/src/KaskadRewardsController.sol#L155-L163

 epochRecycled[epoch][reward] = true;

 uint16 toNextEpochBps = STRATEGY.undistributedToNextEpochBps();
 uint256 toNextEpoch = (undistributed * toNextEpochBps) / 10000;
 uint256 toBurn = undistributed - toNextEpoch;

 if (toNextEpoch > 0) {
     recycledForEpoch[epoch + 1][reward] += toNextEpoch;
 }

The recycledForEpoch mapping is written to but never consumed by any distribution
logic. The next epoch's emission is pulled exclusively from the vault in
EmissionManager._distributeEpochEmission():

 function _distributeEpochEmission(uint256 epoch) internal {
     if (rewardsController == address(0)) revert ZeroAddress();
     uint256 totalEmission = vault.pullForEpoch(epoch, rewardsController);
     // ...
 }

The emissionPerSecond configured via configureAssets() is also derived solely from vaul
t.epochEmission() it does not account for recycled amounts. The KaskadActivityTracker
computes user rewards purely from index growth driven by emissionPerSecond, and never
reads recycledForEpoch.

 The only reader of recycledForEpoch is the view function getRecycledForEpoch(), which
has no callers within the protocol.


Impact
The toNextEpoch portion of undistributed rewards (determined by undistributedToNextEp
ochBps) is neither burned nor redistributed, it remains locked in the KaskadRewardsControl
ler contract.


Recommendation
We need to account for the recycled rewards in the next epoch's reward budget by
increasing the emissionPerSecond for the next epoch such that it reflects the recycled
amount.


Discussion
KaiReytsu
Fixed. Fix details in https://github.com/Kaskad-Lending/kaskad-squashed/pull/8
hildingr
The _maybeDistributePreviousEpoch() flow at KaskadRewardsController.sol:152-165 calls
_autoRecycleEpoch(N) then _updateEmissionRate(N+1) but closeUserEpochs runs after
both (lines 463-466). So _updateEmissionRate sets rolloverApplied[N+1] = true on the
second claim (line 206), and all undistributed generated by subsequent claimers gets
recycled into recycledForEpoch[N+1] (line 184) but never applied to emissions because the
boolean blocks re-entry at line 205.
Recycled rewards are stranded in recycledForEpoch with no mechanism to apply or
recover them.
KaiReytsu
Made the updates. PR: https://github.com/Kaskad-Lending/kaskad-squashed/pull/16

findings.body:
Issue H-7: Attacker can zero out users tvlCompo-
nent by sending a dust amount [RESOLVED]
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2026-02-kaskad-feb-16th-2026/issues/37


Summary
An attacker can permanently zero out any targeted user's tvlComponent voting weight by
front-running their vote() transaction with a dust AToken transfer. This triggers handleAc
tion() → syncParticipation() → _snapshotPositions(), which resets lastSyncTimestamp
to block.timestamp, causing the 1-hour VOTING_COOLDOWN check in _calculateSupplyTerm()
and _calculateBorrowTerm() to return 0. Since the attacker can repeat this on every vote
attempt, the victim's TVL-based governance weight is effectively suppressed indefinitely.


Vulnerability Detail
When a user calls vote(), the governor calls syncForVoting() which was specifically
designed to not update lastSyncTimestamp, then reads the voting weight:
squashed/src/dao/KaskadGovernor.sol#L141-L143

 strategy.syncForVoting(msg.sender);

 uint256 weight = strategy.votingWeight(msg.sender);

The VOTING_COOLDOWN mechanism is intended to prevent flash loan attacks — if lastSyncTi
mestamp was set within the last hour, both _calculateSupplyTerm() and _calculateBorrow
Term() return 0:
squashed/src/dao/KaskadStrategy.sol#L235-L237

 if (state.lastSyncTimestamp + VOTING_COOLDOWN > block.timestamp) {
     return 0;
 }

squashed/src/dao/KaskadStrategy.sol#L265-L267

 if (state.lastSyncTimestamp + VOTING_COOLDOWN > block.timestamp) {
     return 0;
 }


However, there is a separate path that updates lastSyncTimestamp which an attacker
can trigger externally. When any AToken balance changes (including transfers), the
AToken contract calls KaskadRewardsController.handleAction():

 function handleAction(
     address user,
     uint256 totalSupply,
     uint256 userBalance
 ) external override {
     if (address(activityTracker) != address(0)) {
         activityTracker.handleAction(
             msg.sender,
             user,
             totalSupply,
             userBalance
         );
     }
 }

This flows through KaskadActivityTracker.handleAction() which calls STRATEGY.syncParti
cipation(user) at line 144.
syncParticipation() calls _snapshotPositions(), which unconditionally resets the
cooldown timestamp:
squashed/src/dao/KaskadStrategy.sol#L495-L496

 // Record sync timestamp for flash loan protection
 state.lastSyncTimestamp = uint64(block.timestamp);

The attack:
   1. Attacker monitors the mempool for the victim's vote() transaction
  2. Attacker front-runs by transferring a dust amount of ATokens to the victim (e.g. 1
     wei)
  3. The AToken transfer triggers handleAction() → syncParticipation() → _snapshotPos
     itions(), resetting state.lastSyncTimestamp = block.timestamp
  4. The victim's vote() executes in the same block. syncForVoting() does not overwrite
     lastSyncTimestamp, so the cooldown check lastSyncTimestamp + VOTING_COOLDOWN >
     block.timestamp evaluates to true
  5. Both _calculateSupplyTerm() and _calculateBorrowTerm() return 0, zeroing the tvl
     Component
  6. The attacker can repeat this on every vote attempt at negligible cost (dust transfer
     gas)


Note that while syncForVoting() was correctly designed to avoid resetting lastSyncTimes
tamp, this protection is bypassed entirely because the attacker triggers the syncParticip
ation() path externally via a dust AToken transfer.


Impact
Any user's tvlComponent can be zeroed out at will by an attacker front-running their vote
with a dust AToken transfer. Since the attacker can repeat this every time the victim
attempts to vote, the suppression is effectively permanent:
   • Users with significant supply/borrow positions lose their TVL-based governance
     influence entirely.
   • If the victim has no loyalty term (no stKSKD staked), votingWeight() returns 0 and vo
     te() reverts with ZeroWeight(), completely disenfranchising them from governance.
   • The attack cost is negligible (dust AToken transfer gas per vote attempt), while the
     impact is the ability to selectively silence any voter's TVL-weighted governance
     power.


Recommendation
The fix is not straightforward because we want to block flash-loans but we do not want
transfers from other users to zero out our voting. One potential solution is to only reset
the sync timer when the transfer amount is > x% of the user's total position. Dust amount
will not be able to zero-out users TVL. We still block large flashloan attacks as they would
have to be significant to have an impact.
We would have to accept that a x% transfer to a user could reset their TVL component.
We also have to accept that user can manipulate their TVL component by a small
amount with a flashloan under x%.
Alternatively redesign the system with a commit phase such that any increase in their
position after they commit is ignored and require that the commit is => 1h ago, we check
that the current balance is not lower than the balance when we commit.


Discussion
KaiReytsu
Fixed. Fix details in https://github.com/Kaskad-Lending/kaskad-squashed/pull/12

findings.root_cause: Reward emissions are calculated using the user's current scaled balance rather than a time-weighted balance, allowing an eligible user to deposit a large amount just before an epoch ends and receive inflated rewards for the entire epoch.
findings.impact: • Users can receive disproportionately inflated KSKD emission rewards relative to their actual contribution over the epoch. • Honest long-term suppliers who maintain large positions for the full epoch are diluted, as their share of the fixed epoch emissions is reduced by the attacker's inflated claim. • The attack is repeatable every epoch with minimal capital lockup
findings.body:
Issue H-9: Attack can inflate rewards received due
to incorrect balance tracking [RESOLVED]
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2026-02-kaskad-feb-16th-2026/issues/39


Summary
Reward emissions are calculated using the user's current scaled balance rather than a
time-weighted balance, allowing an eligible user to deposit a large amount just before
an epoch ends and receive inflated rewards for the entire epoch.


Vulnerability Detail
supplierEligibleSince is only set once, when a user first crosses the supplierDepositMin
Usd threshold and is never updated on subsequent deposits:
squashed/src/dao/KaskadStrategy.sol#L521-L525

 // Only SET eligibility on entry, never reset here
 // Eligibility reset is handled by ActivityTracker after rewards finalized
 if (state.supplierEligibleSince == 0 && isEligible) {
     state.supplierEligibleSince = uint64(block.timestamp);
 }

When epochs are sealed, rewards are computed using the user's current scaledBalanceOf
not a time-weighted average:
squashed/src/dao/KaskadActivityTracker.sol#L246

 uint256 userBalance = IScaledBalanceToken(asset).scaledBalanceOf(user);

squashed/src/dao/KaskadActivityTracker.sol#L308-L309

 uint256 epochRewards = (ctx.userBalance *
     (endIndex - startIndex)) / ctx.assetUnit;

While handleAction seals past epochs with the pre-transfer (old) balance, the current
epoch remains open and will be sealed later with the new inflated balance:
squashed/src/dao/KaskadActivityTracker.sol#L125-L129

 // 2.5 Seal past epochs using pre-transfer balance (flash loan protection)
 //     handleAction is called BEFORE balance update, so scaledBalanceOf


 //     returns the OLD balance. This locks in correct rewards before
 //     the balance changes.
 _closeForAsset(user, asset, currentEpoch);

_closeForAsset only processes epochs where processedEpoch < ctx.currentEpoch, so the
current epoch is never sealed at deposit time.
Attack scenario:
   1. Day 1 of epoch: User supplies the minimum ($100) to set supplierEligibleSince.
  2. Day 1–29: User maintains the minimum deposit, accumulating uptime past the 90%
     supplier threshold (27 of 30 days).
  3. Day 29: User deposits a much larger amount (e.g. $1M). handleAction seals all past
     epochs with the old balance, but the current epoch remains open.
  4. Next epoch: When the current epoch is eventually sealed (via handleAction or close
     UserEpochs), scaledBalanceOf returns the new large balance, and rewards for the
     entire previous epoch are calculated as $1M_balance * indexGrowth instead of $100
     _balance * indexGrowth.
This is the most capital-efficient execution the attacker only locks minimal capital for
~30 days and a large amount just to front-run the next epoch boundary update.


Impact
   • Users can receive disproportionately inflated KSKD emission rewards relative to
     their actual contribution over the epoch.
   • Honest long-term suppliers who maintain large positions for the full epoch are
     diluted, as their share of the fixed epoch emissions is reduced by the attacker's
     inflated claim.
   • The attack is repeatable every epoch with minimal capital lockup


Recommendation
Use time-weighted balances for reward calculation. For example, track cumulative balan
ce * time per user per epoch and divide by epoch duration when computing rewards.


Discussion
KaiReytsu
Fixed. Fix details in https://github.com/Kaskad-Lending/kaskad-squashed/pull/10
DemoreXTess


Twab causes insolvency and distribute less rewards because index is still calculated by
total supply, system should calculate it accurately, sum of all the twabs should be equal
to divisor value at index calculation.

     .scaledTotalSupply();

 uint256 previousEpochEnd = EpochConfig.end(currentEpoch - 1);

 uint256 index = REWARDS.updateRewardIndexForTracker(
     asset,
     reward,
     actualTotalSupply,

findings.root_cause: The multiple contracts contain an unprotected initialize() function that can be front-run by malicious actors during deployment, potentially causing a Denial of Service (DoS).
findings.impact: An attacker can front-run the initialization with a zero address or invalid address, causing the contract to be permanently misconfigured. Since the initializer modifier prevents re-initialization, the contract would need to be redeployed.
findings.body:
Issue M-1: Contracts can be initialized by anyone
[ACKNOWLEDGED]
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2026-02-kaskad-feb-16th-2026/issues/21
This issue has been acknowledged by the team but won't be fixed at this time.


Summary
The multiple contracts contain an unprotected initialize() function that can be front-run
by malicious actors during deployment, potentially causing a Denial of Service (DoS).


Vulnerability Detail
The initialize() function on line 68 lacks access control restrictions. While it uses
OpenZeppelin's initializer modifier to prevent re-initialization, anyone can call this
function after contract deployment:

 function initialize(address growthPool) external initializer {

The function is intended to be called by the deployer to set the GROWTH_POOL_ROLE,
but since it's publicly callable, an attacker monitoring the mempool can front-run the
legitimate initialization transaction.


Impact
An attacker can front-run the initialization with a zero address or invalid address,
causing the contract to be permanently misconfigured. Since the initializer modifier
prevents re-initialization, the contract would need to be redeployed.


Tool Used
Manual Review


Recommendation
Add access control to the initialize() function by restricting it to only be callable by an
admin role or the deployer.


Discussion
KaiReytsu

 Acknowledged. All initialize() functions use the OpenZeppelin initializer modifier,
guaranteeing single-use execution. If front-run, the deployer's call reverts, the attack is
immediately detected and the contract is redeployed. At initialization time the
contracts are not yet wired into the protocol, so no funds or state are at risk.

findings.body:
Issue M-2: Incomplete Budget Distribution Design
[RESOLVED]
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2026-02-kaskad-feb-16th-2026/issues/22


Summary
The GrowthPool contract's release schedule mathematically cannot distribute 100% of
the totalBudget, leaving approximately 10.9% of funds permanently locked in the
contract.


Vulnerability Detail
The release rate constants sum to only 89.1% of the total budget:
   1. TGE Release: 5.7%
  2. Monthly Releases: 17 months × 4% = 68%
  3. Small Milestones (levels 1-3): 3 × 1.4% = 4.2%
  4. Large Milestones (levels 4-7): 4 × 2.8% = 11.2%
  5. Total: 89.1%
There is no mechanism to release or recover the remaining 10.9% of the budget.


Impact
Approximately 10.9% of the totalBudget will remain permanently locked in the contract
with no way to distribute or recover it.


Tool Used
Manual Review


Recommendation
Adjust the release rate constants to sum to 100%, add a final release mechanism that
distributes remaining funds after all milestones and monthly releases are complete

findings.title: Reward Rate Not Updated on Distribu- tion [RESOLVED]
findings.root_cause: The GrowthPool contract distributes tokens to KaskadRewardsController via direct transfers, but this mechanism fails to update the reward emission rate in the controller, causing distributed tokens to become inaccessible or improperly distributed to users.
findings.impact: Tokens transferred to the rewardsController may sit idle without being distributed to TVL participants, effectively locking protocol funds.
findings.body:
Issue M-3: Reward Rate Not Updated on Distribu-
tion [RESOLVED]
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2026-02-kaskad-feb-16th-2026/issues/23


Summary
The GrowthPool contract distributes tokens to KaskadRewardsController via direct
transfers, but this mechanism fails to update the reward emission rate in the controller,
causing distributed tokens to become inaccessible or improperly distributed to users.


Vulnerability Detail
When triggerMonthlyRelease(), triggerTGE(), or triggerMilestone() are called, the
_distribute() function sends tokens to the rewardsController via safeTransfer:

 if (toTvl > 0) {
     kskd.safeTransfer(rewardsController, toTvl);
 }

However, simply transferring tokens to the KaskadRewardsController does not
automatically update the reward rate per second or notify the controller of new
available rewards. The controller likely maintains internal accounting of emissions and
reward rates that must be explicitly updated when new funds arrive.


Impact
Tokens transferred to the rewardsController may sit idle without being distributed to TVL
participants, effectively locking protocol funds.


Tool Used
Manual Review


Recommendation
Implement a callback mechanism or dedicated function on the
KaskadRewardsController that the GrowthPool calls after transferring tokens. This
function should update the internal reward rate accounting to reflect the newly
available funds for distribution. Consider using a pattern like notifyRewardAmount()
commonly seen in staking reward contracts.

 Discussion
KaiReytsu
Fixed. Fix details in https://github.com/Kaskad-Lending/kaskad-squashed/pull/3

findings.title: Missing Quorum Requirement Allows Single- Voter Decision Control [ACKNOWLEDGED]
findings.root_cause: The KaskadGovernor contract lacks a minimum quorum requirement for governance decisions, allowing a single voter to unilaterally determine protocol parameters by voting at the last moment of a voting window when no other votes have been cast.
findings.impact: An attacker can monitor voting activity and strategically vote at the end of the voting window for decisions with zero participation, setting critical protocol parameters to their preferred values.
findings.body:
Issue M-4: Missing Quorum Requirement Allows Single-
Voter Decision Control [ACKNOWLEDGED]
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2026-02-kaskad-feb-16th-2026/issues/24
This issue has been acknowledged by the team but won't be fixed at this time.


Summary
The KaskadGovernor contract lacks a minimum quorum requirement for governance
decisions, allowing a single voter to unilaterally determine protocol parameters by voting
at the last moment of a voting window when no other votes have been cast.


Vulnerability Detail
The vote() function and finalizeEpoch() function do not implement any quorum checks.
When finalizing an epoch, if totalWeight for a decision is zero (no votes cast), the system
defaults to p.minBps:

 uint256 totalWeight = sumWeights[epoch][d];
 uint16 value = p.minBps;
 if (totalWeight > 0) {
     value = uint16(sumWeightedValues[epoch][d] / totalWeight);
 }

This means any single voter regardless of how small their voting weight—can determine a
decision's outcome if they are the only participant.


Impact
An attacker can monitor voting activity and strategically vote at the end of the voting
window for decisions with zero participation, setting critical protocol parameters to their
preferred values.


Tool Used
Manual Review


Recommendation
Implement a minimum quorum requirement that must be met for a vote to be considered
valid. If the quorum is not reached, either use the previous epoch's values, apply a
default safe value, or extend the voting period. Consider setting the quorum as a

 percentage of total voting power in the system to ensure meaningful participation
before critical parameter changes are enacted.


Discussion
KaiReytsu
Acknowledged. The absence of a quorum is an intentional design choice. A voter cannot
set an arbitrary value, vote() reverts if valueBps falls outside [minBps, maxBps]. The
ranges are hardcoded. Even a single voter with minimal weight cannot exceed these
bounds. When no votes are cast, minBps applies as the most conservative default.

findings.title: Emissions are equal for all assets inde- pendent off their TVL [RESOLVED]
findings.root_cause: EmissionManager.configureAssets() distributes KSKD reward emissions equally across all configured assets regardless of their TVL, allowing rational actors to concentrate deposits in low-TVL pools to capture disproportionately high reward APY.
findings.impact: • Protocol emission budget is spent inefficiently, rewarding low-TVL pools that contribute little to overall protocol health. • Rational users are incentivized to migrate liquidity away from core lending markets into low-TVL pools, degrading the protocol's primary utility.
findings.body:
Issue M-5: Emissions are equal for all assets inde-
pendent off their TVL [RESOLVED]
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2026-02-kaskad-feb-16th-2026/issues/32


Summary
EmissionManager.configureAssets() distributes KSKD reward emissions equally across all
configured assets regardless of their TVL, allowing rational actors to concentrate
deposits in low-TVL pools to capture disproportionately high reward APY.


Vulnerability Detail
In EmissionManager.configureAssets(), the total epoch emission is divided equally
among all assets:
https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2026-02-kaskad-feb-16th-2026/blob/main/kaskad-
squashed/src/dao/EmissionManager.sol#L77-L79

 uint88 emissionPerSecond = uint88(
     epochEmission / DURATION / assets.length
 );

This same emissionPerSecond is then assigned to every asset in the config loop. The Aave
RewardsController distributes rewards proportionally to each user's share of an asset's to
talSupply. Because every pool receives identical emissions, a pool with $100K TVL emits
the same KSKD per second as a pool with $100M TVL — meaning depositors in the small
pool earn ~1000x the reward APY.


Impact
   • Protocol emission budget is spent inefficiently, rewarding low-TVL pools that
     contribute little to overall protocol health.
   • Rational users are incentivized to migrate liquidity away from core lending markets
     into low-TVL pools, degrading the protocol's primary utility.


Recommendation
Weight emissionPerSecond per asset based on TVL or governance-set allocation weights
rather than dividing equally.
Alternatively, introduce a gauge-style weighting system (similar to Curve) where
governance or token holders vote on per-asset emission allocation each epoch.

 Discussion
KaiReytsu
Fixed. Fix details in https://github.com/Kaskad-Lending/kaskad-squashed/pull/6
DemoreXTess
Rates will be updated two times for growth pool, growth pool already increase the rate

findings.title: Un-stake penalty can be circumvented with sybil accounts [ACKNOWLEDGED]
findings.root_cause: StKSKDVault's partial unstake time penalty can be fully bypassed by splitting a stake across multiple accounts (Sybil), allowing users to unstake portions without any entryTim e penalty on remaining funds.
findings.impact: • The partial unstake time penalty in StKSKDVault becomes ineffective as any user can trivially avoid it by using multiple addresses. • Users who split across accounts retain full voting power on remaining stakes, gaining an unfair governance advantage over honest single-account stakers who suffer the intended penalty.
findings.body:
Issue M-6: Un-stake penalty can be circumvented
with sybil accounts [ACKNOWLEDGED]
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2026-02-kaskad-feb-16th-2026/issues/33
This issue has been acknowledged by the team but won't be fixed at this time.


Summary
StKSKDVault's partial unstake time penalty can be fully bypassed by splitting a stake
across multiple accounts (Sybil), allowing users to unstake portions without any entryTim
e penalty on remaining funds.


Vulnerability Detail
When a user partially unstakes from StKSKDVault, the contract penalizes the remaining
balance by shifting entryTime forward proportionally to the fraction withdrawn:
https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2026-02-kaskad-feb-16th-2026/blob/main/kaskad-
squashed/src/pools/StKSKDVault.sol#L74-L80

 } else {
     // Partial unstake — shift entry time forward (lose accumulated time)
     uint64 oldEntry = entryTime[msg.sender];
     uint64 elapsed = uint64(block.timestamp) - oldEntry;
     uint64 timeLost = uint64((uint256(elapsed) * shares) / oldShares);
     entryTime[msg.sender] = oldEntry + timeLost;
 }

This mechanism is designed so that withdrawing a portion of staked tokens reduces the
holding duration (and therefore voting power) on the remaining tokens. However, this
penalty is applied per-address and can be completely avoided by distributing tokens
across multiple accounts before staking.
Example scenario:
A user wants to stake 1000 KSKD but retain the ability to partially exit without penalty:
   1. User splits 1000 KSKD across 10 accounts (100 KSKD each) and stakes on all 10.
  2. After accumulating time D, the user wants to withdraw 10% (100 KSKD).
  3. They fully unstake from one account — entryTime resets to 0 on that account only.
  4. The other 9 accounts retain holdingDuration = D with zero penalty.
The penalty is entirely circumvented. This advantage compounds with repeated partial
withdrawals — a Sybil user can unstake incrementally while always preserving 100% of
accumulated time on remaining funds.

 Impact
   • The partial unstake time penalty in StKSKDVault becomes ineffective as any user
     can trivially avoid it by using multiple addresses.
   • Users who split across accounts retain full voting power on remaining stakes,
     gaining an unfair governance advantage over honest single-account stakers who
     suffer the intended penalty.


Recommendation
This is hard to mitigate since we can not track sybil accounts. The simplest solution is to
remove the penality when unstaking so that normal users also retain their voting power.


Discussion
KaiReytsu
Acknowledged. Sybil attacks (splitting stakes across multiple wallets) are a fundamental
limitation of pseudonymous on-chain accounts that cannot be solved without making
stKSKD non-transferable, which would break composability. The penalty mechanism
uses a weighted-average formula that correctly reduces accumulated time
proportionally on unstake. The penalty increases the cost of single-wallet manipulation,
and any interaction within a single account is correctly pro-rated.

findings.title: User could receive rewards they are not entitled to if no activity happen during an epoch [RESOLVED]
findings.root_cause: Coalesced snapshots in KaskadActivityTracker._snapshotEpoch() bypass per-epoch eligibility checks, allowing users who were ineligible for a given epoch to receive that epoch's full rewards by having them bundled under a later epoch's eligibility check.
findings.impact: Users who are ineligible for a given epoch (due to insufficient uptime) receive that epoch's full rewards when those rewards get coalesced into a later epoch's snapshot. The leaked amount equals the entire epoch's emissions proportional to the user's balance, not merely a partial-epoch fraction.
findings.body:
Issue M-7: User could receive rewards they are not
entitled to if no activity happen during an epoch
[RESOLVED]
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2026-02-kaskad-feb-16th-2026/issues/40


Summary
Coalesced snapshots in KaskadActivityTracker._snapshotEpoch() bypass per-epoch
eligibility checks, allowing users who were ineligible for a given epoch to receive that
epoch's full rewards by having them bundled under a later epoch's eligibility check.


Vulnerability Detail
When no interaction occurs on an asset for an entire epoch, _snapshotEpoch() only
records a snapshot for currentEpoch - 1, skipping all intermediate epochs:

 uint256 targetEpoch = currentEpoch - 1;
 epochIndexSnapshot[asset][reward][targetEpoch] = index;

This single snapshot accumulates the full index delta for every skipped epoch. When
_processEpochsForReward() later processes the user's rewards, it calls
_findNextSnapshot() which scans forward from lastClaimedEpoch and lands on the single
coalesced snapshot. Eligibility is then checked only once, for that snapshot's epoch:

 bool eligible = _isUserEligibleForEpoch(ctx, snapshotEpoch);

No eligibility check is performed for the skipped epochs whose emissions are bundled
into this snapshot.
Scenario:
   1. User deposits late in epoch 7, well below the uptime threshold for epoch 7 eligibility
  2. handleAction fires: epoch 6 is snapshotted, userIndex is set to the epoch 6
     boundary index, lastClaimedEpoch = 7
  3. No interactions occur on this asset during the entirety of epoch 8
  4. In epoch 9, another user interacts with the asset. _snapshotEpoch records only
     epoch 8 (targetEpoch = 9 - 1 = 8). Epoch 7 receives no snapshot
  5. The first user's rewards are processed: _findNextSnapshot(7, 9) finds no snapshot
     at epoch 7, returns epoch 8
  6. The full index delta (covering all of epoch 7 and epoch 8 emissions) is checked
     against epoch 8 eligibility only

   7. The user was present for all of epoch 8, passes the uptime threshold for epoch 8,
     and receives the combined rewards, including the full epoch 7 emissions they were
     never eligible for


Impact
Users who are ineligible for a given epoch (due to insufficient uptime) receive that
epoch's full rewards when those rewards get coalesced into a later epoch's snapshot.
The leaked amount equals the entire epoch's emissions proportional to the user's
balance, not merely a partial-epoch fraction.


Recommendation
When snapshotting after a gap, create snapshots for each skipped epoch individually so
that _processEpochsForReward can check eligibility per epoch.


Discussion
KaiReytsu
Fixed. Fix details in https://github.com/Kaskad-Lending/kaskad-squashed/pull/11

findings.title: Following epoch will receive less emissions than expected when snapShot() is called late [RE- SOLVED]
findings.root_cause: Late epoch snapshots in KaskadActivityTracker._snapshotEpoch() cause the following epoch to receive fewer rewards than intended, because lastUpdateTimestamp is advanced to block.timestamp rather than the previous epoch's end boundary.
findings.impact: An epoch receives less rewards than expected because the index calculation uses an incorrect start time, skipping the period between the epoch's actual start and the delayed snapshot of the prior epoch.
findings.body:
Issue M-8: Following epoch will receive less emissions
than expected when snapShot() is called late [RE-
SOLVED]
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2026-02-kaskad-feb-16th-2026/issues/41


Summary
Late epoch snapshots in KaskadActivityTracker._snapshotEpoch() cause the following
epoch to receive fewer rewards than intended, because lastUpdateTimestamp is
advanced to block.timestamp rather than the previous epoch's end boundary.


Vulnerability Detail
When a user interacts with the protocol after an epoch boundary,
_maybeSnapshotPreviousEpoch() triggers _snapshotEpoch() to record the global reward
index for the most recently completed epoch:

 uint256 index = REWARDS.updateRewardIndexForTracker(
     asset,
     reward,
     actualTotalSupply
 );

 uint256 targetEpoch = currentEpoch - 1;
 epochIndexSnapshot[asset][reward][targetEpoch] = index;

updateRewardIndexForTracker() calls Aave's _updateRewardData(), which updates the
index via _getAssetIndex():

 uint256 currentTimestamp = block.timestamp > distributionEnd
     ? distributionEnd
     : block.timestamp;
 uint256 timeDelta = currentTimestamp - lastUpdateTimestamp;
 uint256 firstTerm = emissionPerSecond * timeDelta * assetUnit;

After computing the new index, _updateRewardData() sets:

 rewardData.lastUpdateTimestamp = block.timestamp.toUint32();

This is the root cause. lastUpdateTimestamp is advanced to block.timestamp which is
already inside the current epoch. When the current epoch is later snapshotted, its index
delta is computed from this advanced lastUpdateTimestamp, not from the actual epoch

 start. The current epoch permanently loses the emissions for the time window between
its start and the moment the late snapshot occurred.


Impact
An epoch receives less rewards than expected because the index calculation uses an
incorrect start time, skipping the period between the epoch's actual start and the
delayed snapshot of the prior epoch.


Recommendation
Enforce epoch-boundary-aware index updates. When snapshotting a completed epoch,
clamp lastUpdateTimestamp to that epoch's end timestamp so that the index delta for
each epoch strictly covers only the time within its boundaries.


Discussion
KaiReytsu
Fixed. Fix details in https://github.com/Kaskad-Lending/kaskad-squashed/pull/5

findings.title: Permits Will Break After Calling ChangeNameAndSymbol
findings.root_cause: The NativeLBTC contract imports ERC20PermitUpgradeable, which adds the EIP-2612 permit() function to enable gasless approvals. However, the function _changeNameAndSymbol allows changes to the token $.name and $.symbol, but does not modify EIP712712Storage._name, which is used in permit.
findings.body:
### Permits Will Break After Calling ChangeNameAndSymbol

The NativeLBTC contract imports ERC20PermitUpgradeable, which adds the EIP-2612 permit() function to enable gasless approvals. However, the function _changeNameAndSymbol allows changes to the token $.name and $.symbol, but does not modify EIP712712Storage._name, which is used in permit.

This change would break all new permit() calls, which would end up reverting, because ERC20Permit.domainSeparator() would still use the previous name.

Consider either removing the option to modify the token name and symbol or implementing a reinitialize function that invokes the _EIP712_init function with the updated name.

Update: Resolved in pull request #225.

## Medium Severity

findings.title: Signatures Can Be Reused
findings.root_cause: In the NativeLBTC.sol contract, the _mintV1WithFee function validates user signatures authorizing fee payments. However, the function does not have any mechanism to prevent signature replays.
findings.body:
### Signatures Can Be Reused

In the NativeLBTC.sol contract, the _mintV1WithFee function validates user signatures authorizing fee payments. However, the function does not have any mechanism to prevent signature replays.

As a result, the same (feePayload, userSignature) pair can be reused multiple times by any address with CLAIMER_ROLE, granting them the ability to repeatedly deduct fees from a user for any future deposits, until the fee expiry time, to the same recipient. Additionally, since the fee approval is not bound to a specific deposit payload, any valid feePayload can be combined with any deposit payload as long as the recipient matches.

Although the total minted amount remains consistent with the underlying deposit and does not result in extra tokens minted, the design allows non-revocable fee permissions, valid for a specified time interval, that may be unintuitive for users and diverge from the EIP-2612 patterns which expect single-use signatures.

Consider introducing a per-user nonce to ensure each signature is used only once and binding fee approvals more tightly to the intended context to prevent unauthorized or unintended reuse.

Update: Acknowledged, not resolved. The Lombard team stated:

It is intentional design, user provide approve(signature) not for the specific deposit but for the specific time and can do many deposits during this time or do not do any deposits.

findings.title: Missing Lower Bound on User Specified Fees in Minting
findings.root_cause: The address holding the CLAIMER_ROLE can mint NativeLBTC by calling mintV1WithFee or batchMintV1WithFee, providing a DepositBtcActionV1 payload signed by the validators and a feePayload, signed by the user who will receive the tokens. However, the actual fee applied is the minimum of the maximumFee, set by the contract owner, and the fee specified by the user in the signed feePayload.
findings.body:
### Missing Lower Bound on User Specified Fees in Minting

The address holding the CLAIMER_ROLE can mint NativeLBTC by calling mintV1WithFee or batchMintV1WithFee, providing a DepositBtcActionV1 payload signed by the validators and a feePayload, signed by the user who will receive the tokens. However, the actual fee applied is the minimum of the maximumFee, set by the contract owner, and the fee specified by the user in the signed feePayload.

While the contract ensures that the fee signed by the user is not zero, it can be set to arbitrarily small values (e.g., 1 wei). In such cases, this minimal fee would be applied (even if maximumFee is not zero), rendering the fee mechanism ineffective in preventing denial of service (DoS) attacks, which is its primary intended purpose.

Consider enforcing a minimum fee threshold (at least when maximumFee is not zero) to ensure the minting fee remains an effective mechanism against DoS attacks.

Update: Acknowledged, not resolved. The Lombard team stated:

User can provide any fee level that he is ready to pay, but it is claimer decision if he is ready to claim for such fee. There are no guarantee that it will be claimed with any fee. Moreover gas price can be changed and if before fee level was too small, maybe some hours later will be ok.

## Low Severity

findings.title: Revoking a vesting grant takes vested tokens away
findings.root_cause: The revoke function in VestingTrustee allows the owner to revoke an address’s vesting grant, in the case that it is revocable. This consists of erasing the grant and transferring the remaining tokens to the owner.
findings.body:
#### Revoking a vesting grant takes vested tokens away

The revoke function in VestingTrustee allows the owner to revoke an address’s vesting grant, in the case that it is revocable. This consists of erasing the grant and transferring the remaining tokens to the owner. The function considers “remaining tokens” to be all those that haven’t been unlocked and transferred yet. However, it is likely that remaining tokens should be considered to be only those which have not yet vested, regardless of whether they’ve been transferred or not. Consider changing revoke to first transfer vested tokens to the grantee, and only the remaining as a refund to the owner.

Update: The team assured us that, although they have not implemented our suggested change, the risk is mitigated by the fact that all vesting grants will be made irrevocable as soon as possible after the sale and that revocation will be only possible by getting access to the multisig owner of the contract. There is no risk for an irrevocable grant, so there would be no problem for investors after made irrevocable.

### High Severity

findings.body:
#### Unexpected value for MAX_TOKENS_SOLD

The state variable MAX_TOKENS_SOLD in KinTokenSale represents the maximum number of tokens to be sold during the crowdsale, which is defined to be 1 trillion according to the whitepaper (chapter 6, Kin token issuance). However, the value in the contract is 512192121951 (slightly above half a trillion). Update this constant to reflect the value indicated in the whitepaper.

findings.title: Token ownership can be transferred while minting
findings.root_cause: The KinTokenSale contract allows the owner to transfer the token ownership to a different address at any moment, using the function requestKinTokenOwnershipTransfer. Since the token is in a minting state during the sale (i.e. new tokens can be created by the owner), this harms the trustlessness of the contract, as it would allow the owner to mint themselves an arbitrary number of tokens, against what was established in paper.
findings.body:
#### Token ownership can be transferred while minting

The KinTokenSale contract allows the owner to transfer the token ownership to a different address at any moment, using the function requestKinTokenOwnershipTransfer. Since the token is in a minting state during the sale (i.e. new tokens can be created by the owner), this harms the trustlessness of the contract, as it would allow the owner to mint themselves an arbitrary number of tokens, against what was established in paper.

A comment next to the function correctly states that transferring token ownership would prevent the token sale to continue operating. If such a thing happened, the function acceptKinTokenOwnership would allow the sale to become the token owner again, and continue operating. However, in the meantime, an owner could end the minting phase of the token manually, violating the explicit requirement that grants be distributed before minting is ended, and that this be done after the sale period.

We recommend to remove the functions requestKinTokenOwnershipTransfer and acceptKinTokenOwnership, as they are not needed and compromise the correctness and security of the sale.

Update: The team replied that the owner will be a multisig wallet, which mitigates the risk. Due to time constraints, the functions will be kept as the only method to pause the sale in an emergency.

findings.title: All vesting grants are revocable
findings.root_cause: It should be noted that all vesting grants are revocable (indicated by the last parameter, true), including the large grant given to Kik. If a grant is revoked, all of its vesting tokens are immediately transferred to the owner of VestingTrustee.
findings.body:
#### All vesting grants are revocable

It should be noted that all vesting grants are revocable (indicated by the last parameter, true), including the large grant given to Kik. If a grant is revoked, all of its vesting tokens are immediately transferred to the owner of VestingTrustee. Make sure that this is in fact desired.

Update: The team has clarified that this is a temporary measure so that possible errors can be fixed afterwards, and that all grants will be manually made irrevocable as soon as possible.

### Medium Severity

findings.title: Participation caps can be altered mid-crowdsale
findings.root_cause: The functions setTier1Participants, setTier2Participants, and setHardParticipationCap allow the owner of the token sale contract to modify the cap for any participant at any point in time, even after the crowdsale has started. To improve the public trust on the sale mechanics, it is recommended that once the sale starts, all caps are frozen and cannot be modified.
findings.body:
#### Participation caps can be altered mid-crowdsale

The functions setTier1Participants, setTier2Participants, and setHardParticipationCap allow the owner of the token sale contract to modify the cap for any participant at any point in time, even after the crowdsale has started. To improve the public trust on the sale mechanics, it is recommended that once the sale starts, all caps are frozen and cannot be modified. Consider adding an onlyBeforeSale modifier to these functions.

Update: The team explained that this is intentional so that potential errors in the KYC process can be corrected by changing a participant’s tier at any moment.

findings.title: Possible to transfer more balance than necessary to VestingTrustee
findings.root_cause: It should be noted that it is possible to transfer more token balance than necessary to VestingTrustee. In that case, the only way to recover the surplus is to create a new grant that allows to immediately unlock its full amount.
findings.body:
#### Possible to transfer more balance than necessary to VestingTrustee

It should be noted that it is possible to transfer more token balance than necessary to VestingTrustee. In that case, the only way to recover the surplus is to create a new grant that allows to immediately unlock its full amount. Although this is not a problem in the context of the trustee managed by the token sale contract, it could be inconvenient if VestingTrustee were to be used by itself.

### Low Severity

findings.body:
[M-1] Incorrect fee calculation due to use of `msg.sender` in `_collectFees` function

  Severity: Medium                              Status: Resolved

Context:

     PositionRouter.sol#L437

Description:

When a user's increasePosition request is executed, he should pay additional fees based
on the status of his existing position:


        function _collectFees(
            address _account,
            address[] memory _path,
            uint256 _amountIn,
            address _indexToken,
            bool _isLong,
            uint256 _sizeDelta
        ) internal returns (uint256) {
            bool shouldDeductFee = _shouldDeductFee(
   >>               _account,
                    _path,
                    _amountIn,
                    _indexToken,
                    _isLong,
                    _sizeDelta
               );




However, when the _collectFees function is called within executeIncreasePosition,
msg.sender is used instead of account.request. This causes the fee calculation to be based
on the caller's account data, not the original request creator’s. As a result, fees could be
applied incorrectly.

Recommendation:

        function executeIncreasePosition(bytes32 _key, address payable
   _executionFeeReceiver) public nonReentrant returns (bool) {
               ---SNIP---
   +           uint256 afterFeeAmount = _collectFees(request.account,
   request.path, amountIn, request.indexToken, request.isLong,
   request.sizeDelta);

[M-3] `priceFeedSetTokenConfig()` will always fail due to incorrect `action` hash in
`signalPriceFeedSetTokenConfig()`

  Severity: Medium                           Status: Resolved

Context:
     LiqTimelock.sol#L468-L485
     LiqTimelock.sol#L63-L69

Description:
The action hash for signalPriceFeedSetTokenConfig() is created using pyth variables
instead of chainlink variables. This will cause a mismatch for the
priceFeedSetTokenConfig(), preventing it from working. The emit
SignalPriceFeedSetTokenConfig() is also incorrect.


       function signalPriceFeedSetTokenConfig(
           address _vaultPriceFeed,
           address _token,
   >>>     bool _isStrictStable,
   >>>     bytes32 _pythPriceId,
   >>>     uint256 _pythConfScalingFactor
       ) external onlyAdmin {
           bytes32 action = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(
               "priceFeedSetTokenConfig",
               _vaultPriceFeed,
               _token,
   >>>         _isStrictStable,
   >>>         _pythPriceId,
   >>>         _pythConfScalingFactor
           ));

               _setPendingAction(action);

               emit SignalPriceFeedSetTokenConfig(
                    _vaultPriceFeed,
                    _token,
   >>>              _isStrictStable,
   >>>              _pythPriceId,
   >>>              _pythConfScalingFactor
               );
         }

 Recommendation:


           function signalPriceFeedSetTokenConfig(
               address _vaultPriceFeed,
               address _token,
   -            bool _isStrictStable,
   -            bytes32 _pythPriceId,
   -            uint256 _pythConfScalingFactor
   +            address _priceFeed,
   +            uint256 _priceDecimals,
   +            bool _isStrictStable
           ) external onlyAdmin {
               bytes32 action = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(
                   "priceFeedSetTokenConfig",
                   _vaultPriceFeed,
                   _token,
   -                _isStrictStable,
   -                _pythPriceId,
   -                _pythConfScalingFactor
   +                _priceFeed,
   +                _priceDecimals,
   +                _isStrictStable
               ));

               _setPendingAction(action);

               emit SignalPriceFeedSetTokenConfig(
                   _vaultPriceFeed,
                   _token,
   -                _isStrictStable,
       -            _pythPriceId,
       -            _pythConfScalingFactor
   +                _priceFeed,
   +                _priceDecimals,
   +                _isStrictStable
               );
           }

findings.title: Insufficient Account Checks
findings.root_cause: The codebase contains a broad class of vulnerabilities related to insufficient validation of intermediate accounts passed via remaining_accounts . These vulnerabilities may enable malicious actors to spoof the sender or manipulate other critical account details, leading to unauthorized actions or token transfers.
findings.body:
Insufficient Account Checks MEDIUM    OS-LZS-ADV-02

Description

The codebase contains a broad class of vulnerabilities related to insufficient validation of intermediate
accounts passed via remaining_accounts . These vulnerabilities may enable malicious actors to
spoof the sender or manipulate other critical account details, leading to unauthorized actions or token
transfers. This issue is particularly pertinent in the context of the OFT (Omnichain Fungible Token) CPI
(Cross-Program Invocation) within the endpoint for sending transactions.

The send::apply function uses CPI to interact with the endpoint program, providing transac-
tion details such as the destination endpoint, receiver, message, and associated fees. It also passes
remaining_accounts . Without proper validation of these accounts, an attacker could insert a spoofed
sender account, making it appear as though a legitimate user is initiating the transaction. In reality, the
attacker would be in control, potentially leading to unauthorized transfers or actions.

Remediation

Validate that each account in remaining_accounts corresponds to the expected signer address.

Patch

Fixed in 101ae40.

findings.body:
[H-2] when cachedTokenAllocationBps decreases , investors can maliciously use the
old cachedTokenAllocationBps before refund

  Severity: High                            Status: Resolved

Context:
     LegionPreLiquidSale.sol#L416
     LegionPreLiquidSale.sol#L512

Description:
the project can modify the terms by updatingVestingTerms() and
updateSAFTMerkleRoot().

For example, it is possible to reduce an investor's investment percentage, and after updating
the terms, that investor can get back the ExcessCapital by withdrawExcessCapital().
But currently there is no restriction on the order of claimAskTokenAllocation() and
withdrawExcessCapital().

This way, a malicious investor can execute claimAskTokenAllocation() first and use the
larger cachedTokenAllocationBps to maliciously obtain more askTokens.
After that, execute withdrawExcessCapital() to retrieve the ExcessCapital.
Example:
  1. project call updateSAFTMerkleRoot()
          cachedTokenAllocationBps[alice]= 5%
          cachedSAFTInvestAmount = 500e6
  2. alice call invest(500e6)
  3. project call updateSAFTMerkleRoot()
           cachedTokenAllocationBps[alice]= 1% ----> cachedTokenAllocationBps decreases
           cachedSAFTInvestAmount = 100e6
  4. alice call claimAskTokenAllocation()
           get cachedTokenAllocationBps[alice]= 5% ask token
  5. alice call withdrawExcessCapital()
           get back 400e6 bidToken

Recommendation:

claimAskTokenAllocation() add in proof[] and validate saftMerkleRoot again.

    -   function claimAskTokenAllocation() external {
   +   function claimAskTokenAllocation(bytes32[] calldata proof) external {
            /// Verify that the sale has not been canceled
            _verifySaleNotCanceled();

            /// Verify that the investor can claim the token allocation
            _verifyCanClaimTokenAllocation(msg.sender);

   +        _verifyCanInvestCapital(msg.sender, proof);

[M-1] withdrawCapitalIfSaleIsCanceled() Investors who have already settled can still
refund

  Severity: Medium                              Status: Resolved


Context:
     LegionPreLiquidSale.sol#L486

Description:
If the project owner decides to cancel PreLiquid, it can be done through the method
cancelSale(). When canceling, need to return the withdrawn capital:
totalCapitalWithdrawn. The investor can then retrieve the investment via
withdrawCapitalIfSaleIsCanceled().

The problem is that currently withdrawCapitalIfSaleIsCanceled() doesn't restrict the
refund of already settled investments. This can result in the investor receiving both askToken
+ refund bidToken.
Example:
   1. alice invest 100 bidToken
   2. publishTgeDetails() && supplyAskTokens()
   3. the project call withdrawRaisedCapital() , totalCapitalWithdrawn = 1000
   4. alice claimAskTokenAllocation() , get 100 askToken
   5. the project Decide to cancel ， call cancelSale() , return totalCapitalWithdrawn = 1000
   6. alice call withdrawCapitalIfSaleIsCanceled() get 100 bidToken
so alice get 100 refund bidToken + 100 askToken

Recommendation:
It is recommended that what has been settled cannot be refunded, and the excess bidToken
is returned to the project offline via emergencyWithdraw().



        function withdrawCapitalIfSaleIsCanceled() external {
            /// Verify that the sale has been actually canceled
            _verifySaleIsCanceled();

               /// Cache the amount to refund in memory

            uint256 amountToClaim =
   investorPositions[msg.sender].investedCapital;
   +       if (investorPositions[msg.sender].hasSettled) revert
   AlreadySettled(msg.sender);

findings.body:
Issue M-2: liquidateBurn does not refund closeAmo
unt (excess collateral) to ownerOf(tokenId) [RESOLVED]
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2025-12-likwid-protocol-dec-22nd/issues/57


Summary
In LikwidMarginPosition.liquidateBurn(), the return value closeAmount from MarginPosi
tion.close() is discarded. If a position is liquidatable under the protocol’s liquidation
check, but still has sufficient collateral to fully repay debt (and liquidation fees) at
current pairReserves, MarginPosition.close() can produce a non-zero closeAmount (i.e.,
released collateral minus the collateral cost to repay the debt). The current liquidateBur
n implementation does not transfer this excess collateral back to ownerOf(tokenId);
instead, it is effectively absorbed into pool accounting via pairDelta/lendDelta updates.
This can cause unnecessary user loss during liquidation and may allow actors who can
trigger liquidation (or who are economically exposed to pool reserves as LPs/lenders) to
capture value that should have been returned to the position owner, depending on
intended protocol semantics.


Vulnerability Detail
   • MarginPosition.close() computes an excess-collateral return value closeAmount
     when the released collateral exceeds the collateral required to repay the debt:
       – closeAmount = releaseAmount - costAmount when releaseAmount > costAmount
         . See src/libraries/MarginPosition.sol:158 (notably src/libraries/MarginPo
         sition.sol:201-208).
   • User-initiated closes correctly pay out closeAmount to the caller by including it in ma
     rginDelta and setting pairDelta to consume only releaseAmount - closeAmount
     collateral:
       – See src/LikwidMarginPosition.sol:409 (notably src/LikwidMarginPosition.so
         l:425-446).
   • liquidateBurn() discards closeAmount by destructuring position.close(...) as (re
     leaseAmount, repayAmount,, lostAmount, swapFeeAmount) and never
     credits/transfers any excess collateral:
       – See src/LikwidMarginPosition.sol:475 (notably src/LikwidMarginPosition.so
         l:495-520).
   • Additionally, liquidateBurn() uses pairDelta as if closeAmount == 0 (consuming the
     full releaseAmount as collateral) rather than consuming only releaseAmount - close
     Amount and paying closeAmount out:

        – For marginForOne == true, delta.pairDelta uses -releaseAmount instead of -(r
         eleaseAmount - closeAmount) (compare src/LikwidMarginPosition.sol:510-51
         4 with src/LikwidMarginPosition.sol:437-440).
   • The liquidation callback (_handleLiquidateBurn) only transfers callerProfitAmount
     and protocolProfitAmount, which matches the chosen params.marginDelta = rewar
     dAmount, but leaves no mechanism to transfer any additional amount to the
     position owner:
       – See src/LikwidMarginPosition.sol:689 (notably src/LikwidMarginPosition.so
         l:698-712).
Attack/abuse scenario (economic loss):
   1. A position becomes liquidatable under the protocol’s liquidation check (e.g., due to
      rate-limited/truncated pricing), while at current pairReserves the position’s
      collateral is still sufficient to cover its debt plus rewardAmount.
  2. A third party calls liquidateBurn(tokenId, ...).
  3. MarginPosition.close() computes closeAmount > 0, but liquidateBurn() ignores it,
     and pool deltas are applied as if the entire releaseAmount is consumed.
  4. The position owner receives no refund for the excess collateral; value remains in
     pool reserves (benefiting LPs/lenders/protocol depending on design).


Impact
   • Position owners can lose excess collateral during liquidateBurn liquidations even
     when the position is not economically “underwater” at current pairReserves.
   • The protocol’s intended liquidation economics (penalty bounded to callerProfit +
     protocolProfit, with remainder returned to owner) may be violated, leading to
     user-funds misallocation and trust issues.
   • If liquidators can influence which liquidation path is used (or if liquidators are also
     LPs/lenders), this can create an incentive to liquidate positions to capture/redirect
     value that should have been refunded to the owner.


Code Snippet
https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2025-12-likwid-protocol-dec-22nd/tree/main/likwid-
margin/src/LikwidMarginPosition.sol#L495


Tool Used
Manual Review

 Recommendation
   • Decide and document intended semantics for liquidateBurn regarding surplus
     collateral:
          – If surplus should be returned to the position owner, then:

              * Capture closeAmount in liquidateBurn.
              * Update deltas analogously to close() so that only releaseAmount - closeA
                mount is consumed by the pool and closeAmount is credited in params.margi
                nDelta.

              * Transfer closeAmount to ownerOf(tokenId) inside the unlock callback (e.g.,
                include the owner address in callback params, or use ERC721._requireOwne
                d(tokenId) to fetch it before unlock and pass it through).
          – If surplus is intended to be confiscated, explicitly reflect this in naming/docs
            and emit it in events for transparency (e.g., include closeAmount/surplus in Liqu
            idateBurn event).


Discussion

findings.body:
Issue M-3: liquidateCall does not charge protocol
Profit, and liquidation does not return any surplus
collateral to the position owner [RESOLVED]
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2025-12-likwid-protocol-dec-22nd/issues/58


Summary
Compared to liquidateBurn, LikwidMarginPosition.liquidateCall() does not calculate
or distribute callerProfit / protocolProfit, meaning liquidations executed through the
call-path do not pay the protocol profit that exists in the burn-path. Additionally, liquid
ateCall releases the entire position collateral (marginAmount + marginTotal) but does not
return any potential surplus to the position owner, even in cases where the released
collateral value could exceed the amount needed to cover the debt (e.g., due to pricing
inconsistencies or liquidation being triggered at an unfavorable oracle checkpoint).


Vulnerability Detail
1) No protocolProfit accounting in liquidateCall
   • liquidateBurn explicitly computes and distributes:
       – profit = assetsAmount * callerProfit
       – protocolProfitAmount = assetsAmount * protocolProfit and transfers them
         in _handleLiquidateBurn.
   • liquidateCall does not compute these values, does not transfer them to the
     protocol, and the LiquidateCall event does not include protocol profit fields.
This creates a path-dependent fee behavior: liquidations routed through liquidateCall
avoid protocol profit that is otherwise charged in liquidateBurn, which can skew
incentives and expected revenue.


2) No surplus refund to the position owner
In liquidateCall:
   • profit is set to the full collateral balance: profit = marginAmount + marginTotal.
   • position.update(..., repayAmount=debtAmount) is called, which (for this input)
     releases the full positionValue and sets repayAmount to the full debt amount; the
     function then enforces profit == releaseAmount.
   • The callback applies deltas that transfer releaseAmount (the entire collateral) to the
     liquidator, while the liquidator’s borrow-token payment is capped by realRepayAmou


     nt = min(debtAmount, needPayAmount).
As a result, the position owner is not refunded any remaining collateral, and the entire
collateral is allocated to liquidation settlement flows / liquidator, even if the realized
debt repayment is less than the value of the released collateral at some pricing basis.


Impact
   • Protocol revenue leakage / inconsistent economics: if liquidators can choose
     between liquidateBurn and liquidateCall, they can prefer the path that does not
     pay protocol profit, reducing protocol fee capture compared to expectations.
   • Unfair value transfer from user to liquidator: liquidateCall always confiscates the
     entire collateral and does not return any residual to the position owner. If
     liquidation can be triggered when the position still has positive equity under some
     economic view, the liquidator can capture that residual.
   • Incentive misalignment: when liquidateCall is systematically more profitable (no
     protocol profit + potential residual capture), liquidators will prefer it, potentially
     making liquidateBurn unused and undermining intended fee mechanics.


Code Snippet
   • liquidateCall releases all collateral and does not compute protocol profit:
          main/likwid-margin/src/LikwidMarginPosition.sol#L547 (liquidateCall)
          main/likwid-margin/src/LikwidMarginPosition.sol#L581 (realRepayAmount =
          min(repayAmount, needPayAmount))
   • liquidateBurn computes and pays callerProfit + protocolProfit:
          main/likwid-margin/src/LikwidMarginPosition.sol#L488-L491 (profit
          calculations)


Tool Used
Manual Review


Recommendation
   • Decide and document the intended economics between liquidateBurn and liquida
     teCall. If both are intended liquidation mechanisms, make fee behavior consistent:


          – Add callerProfit / protocolProfit accounting to liquidateCall (or remove it
            from liquidateBurn if not intended).
   • If the intended liquidation design should not confiscate residual equity:
          – Compute the required debt repayment using a manipulation-resistant price,
            repay debt up to the required amount, and return any surplus collateral to the
            position owner (or to a designated recipient).


Discussion

findings.title: MarginPosition.close() bypasses dynamic swap fee, enabling low-cost pool price manipulation [RESOLVED]
findings.root_cause: MarginPosition.close() uses the fixed-fee SwapMath.getAmountOut/getAmountIn overloads (only pairReserves + lpFee) instead of the dynamic-fee overloads that incorporate truncatedReserves and price-impact-based fee scaling. As a result, closing a leveraged position can be used as an alternative “swap path” that moves the pool’s spot price while paying only the base LP fee (i.e., avoiding the intended dynamic fee penalty for large price impact).
findings.impact: • Fee bypass / value leakage: for high-impact closes, the protocol collects less swap fee than intended. The missing portion is effectively value transferred from LPs (and protocol fee recipients) to the closer. • Low-cost price manipulation: an attacker can shift the pool’s spot price via repeated/large closes at a discounted fee rate.
findings.body:
Issue M-4: MarginPosition.close() bypasses dynamic
swap fee, enabling low-cost pool price manipulation
[RESOLVED]
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2025-12-likwid-protocol-dec-22nd/issues/59


Summary
MarginPosition.close() uses the fixed-fee SwapMath.getAmountOut/getAmountIn
overloads (only pairReserves + lpFee) instead of the dynamic-fee overloads that
incorporate truncatedReserves and price-impact-based fee scaling. As a result, closing a
leveraged position can be used as an alternative “swap path” that moves the pool’s spot
price while paying only the base LP fee (i.e., avoiding the intended dynamic fee penalty
for large price impact).


Vulnerability Detail
The protocol implements a dynamic swap fee mechanism in SwapMath:
   • SwapMath.getAmountOut(pairReserves, truncatedReserves, lpFee, ...) and SwapM
     ath.getAmountIn(pairReserves, truncatedReserves, lpFee, ...) compute a degre
     e of price change using truncatedReserves as a checkpoint and apply dynamicFee(l
     pFee, degree) to increase fees as price impact grows (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:
     137).
   • The canonical swap path (Pool.swap) uses these dynamic-fee overloads (src/librar
     ies/Pool.sol:205).


Affected call sites in LikwidMarginPosition
The fixed-fee MarginPosition.close(...) logic is exercised by the following functions in
src/LikwidMarginPosition.sol:
   • close(uint256 tokenId, uint24 closeMillionth, uint256 closeAmountMin, uint25
     6 deadline) (src/LikwidMarginPosition.sol:409) calls position.close(...) (src/Li
     kwidMarginPosition.sol:425).
   • liquidateBurn(uint256 tokenId, uint256 deadline) (src/LikwidMarginPosition.so
     l:476) calls position.close(...) (src/LikwidMarginPosition.sol:495).
However, MarginPosition.close() calculates the close swap amounts and swapFeeAmount
using the fixed-fee overloads:
   • SwapMath.getAmountOut(pairReserves, lpFee, ..., releaseAmount) (src/libraries
     /MarginPosition.sol:196)


   • SwapMath.getAmountIn(pairReserves, lpFee, ..., repayAmount) (src/libraries/Ma
     rginPosition.sol:201)
LikwidMarginPosition.close() then applies the resulting deltas directly via vault.unlock
(...) -> vault.marginBalance(...), updating pool reserves without re-pricing through P
ool.swap (src/LikwidMarginPosition.sol:425). This effectively makes “closing a position”
a fee-discounted swap mechanism compared to the intended dynamic-fee swap path.


Why this enables manipulation
An attacker can intentionally create/maintain debt (so self.debtAmount > 0) and choose
closeMillionth to size the implicit swap performed during close. Because the close
pricing uses only the base lpFee and does not incorporate the dynamic fee increase for
high price impact, the attacker can move pairReserves (and thus spot price) with less
cost than Pool.swap would require for an equivalently large swap.


Impact
   • Fee bypass / value leakage: for high-impact closes, the protocol collects less swap
     fee than intended. The missing portion is effectively value transferred from LPs
     (and protocol fee recipients) to the closer.
   • Low-cost price manipulation: an attacker can shift the pool’s spot price via
     repeated/large closes at a discounted fee rate. This can be used to:
       – Arbitrage against external venues after forcing an unfavorable internal price
         move at low cost.
       – Manipulate other users’ margin level checks or liquidation boundaries that
         depend on pool reserves (depending on where pairReserves/truncatedReserve
         s are referenced).
       – Create cheaper within-protocol MEV/sandwich opportunities around victim
         actions that depend on pool price.
